subtopic_detail: blue episodes provoked by frustration in a toddler whose milk intake has displaced solid food
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 18 month old girl whose mother describes six episodes in three months. Each begins when she is hurt or told no, she cries hard, stops breathing out, turns blue around the lips and goes limp for about twenty seconds, then wakes irritable.

Her mother says two of the episodes ended with a few seconds of stiffening of the arms. There has never been an episode during sleep, during exercise or without an obvious trigger, and she has never been incontinent or drowsy for long afterwards. She walks, runs and says twenty words. She drinks about 1.4 litres of cow milk each day and eats very little meat or cereal. There is no family history of sudden death or of fainting, and her electrocardiogram taken last week was reported as normal with a corrected QT interval of 410 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 124/min, blood pressure 92/54 mmHg, respiratory rate 26/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pale conjunctivae, no murmur, femoral pulses equal, neurological examination normal, weight on the 25th centile and length on the 50th
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram normal with corrected QT interval 410 ms (below 440), no bloods taken

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Supply buccal midazolam for the parents to give during the longer episodes
options.rationale: The episodes are self limiting within a minute and terminate as breathing resumes, so a rescue anticonvulsant treats nothing and exposes a toddler to sedation and airway risk. Rescue medication belongs with prolonged epileptic seizures, not with hypoxic events of this kind. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.text: Reassure the parents that the episodes are harmless and need no further assessment
options.rationale: Reassurance about the benign natural history is correct as far as it goes and is part of the consultation. It is incomplete here because the pallor and the milk intake point to a treatable contributor that reassurance alone will leave in place. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

options.text: Arrange a sleep deprived electroencephalogram to characterise the stiffening movements
options.rationale: Brief stiffening or a few jerks at the end of a prolonged episode is a hypoxic phenomenon and does not indicate epilepsy when every episode has an emotional or painful trigger. An electroencephalogram in this setting is normal or shows non specific findings that risk an incorrect diagnosis. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.text: Refer for 24 hour ambulatory cardiac monitoring before any other investigation
options.rationale: Ambulatory monitoring is directed at episodes occurring without warning, during exercise or during sleep, or where the family history raises the possibility of an inherited arrhythmia. A normal corrected QT interval with a consistent emotional trigger and no relevant family history makes this a low yield test. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Breath holding attacks

options.text: Take a full blood count with iron studies and replace iron if the stores are low
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is found in a large proportion of children with these episodes and treating it reduces both their frequency and their severity, which is the only intervention shown to change the natural history. Her milk intake of 1.4 litres daily displaces iron rich food and inhibits absorption, and she is pale, so the deficiency is likely and worth confirming before it is treated. (Source: RCH CPG: Iron deficiency)

explanation.summary: Blue episodes triggered by pain or frustration in a toddler, with a short recovery and no episodes during sleep or exertion, describe a hypoxic event rather than a seizure or an arrhythmia. Terminal stiffening is common once the episode lasts long enough to cause cerebral hypoxia and does not change the diagnosis. The feature that should change management here is the combination of pallor and a milk intake that has displaced iron rich solids, because iron deficiency is strongly associated with these episodes and its correction reduces them. Confirming the deficiency before treating avoids committing a child to iron on the basis of appearance alone. A normal corrected QT interval and the absence of exertional or sleep related episodes make cardiac investigation low yield.
key_points: Every episode following a trigger, with recovery in under a minute, argues against epilepsy.
Terminal stiffening reflects cerebral hypoxia and does not warrant an electroencephalogram.
Cow milk above about 500 mL daily in a toddler displaces iron rich foods and impairs absorption.
Correcting iron deficiency reduces the frequency and severity of these episodes.
Episodes during sleep or exertion, or a family history of sudden death, shift the workup to cardiac.
explanation.pearls: Ask the daily milk volume in every toddler presenting with these episodes, because intake above 500 mL a day makes iron deficiency likely, and replacing iron for three months is the one intervention that reduces how often the episodes happen.

subtopic_detail: a visible cervical abnormality that must not be accepted as the cause of bleeding without exclusion
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 23 year old woman with three months of spotting after intercourse and occasional light bleeding between periods. She started the combined oral contraceptive pill five months ago and takes it reliably at the same time each day.

She has a new partner of four months and they use the pill alone for contraception. She has no pelvic pain, no discharge that she has noticed, no fevers and no weight loss. Her only cervical screening test was two years ago and reported no oncogenic human papillomavirus. On speculum examination there is a symmetrical ring of red velvety tissue extending from the external os onto the surrounding cervix, which bleeds lightly when touched by the swab. The uterus is normal sized and mobile with no adnexal mass or cervical motion tenderness.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical circumferential red velvety area around the external os bleeding on contact, no ulceration, no irregular mass, uterus normal size and mobile, no adnexal mass or cervical motion tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Cervical screening two years ago negative for oncogenic human papillomavirus, pregnancy test negative today
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill containing 30 micrograms of ethinyloestradiol

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Take endocervical and vaginal swabs for chlamydia and gonorrhoea before attributing the bleeding
options.rationale: The appearance describes columnar epithelium extended onto the outer cervix, which is a normal finding in a young woman on oestrogen containing contraception and bleeds easily on contact. It is a common but unreliable explanation for the symptom, so infection must be excluded first, and chlamydial cervicitis in a woman with a new partner produces exactly this pattern of bleeding with no discharge or pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

options.text: Refer for colposcopy because contact bleeding requires exclusion of cervical malignancy
options.rationale: Colposcopy is indicated for an irregular, ulcerated or friable mass, for persistent bleeding after infection has been excluded and treated, or for an abnormal screening result. A negative human papillomavirus test two years ago makes significant cervical disease very unlikely, and a symmetrical circumferential appearance is not the pattern of malignancy. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Reassure her that the appearance is benign and review her only if the bleeding persists
options.rationale: The appearance genuinely is benign and does not itself require treatment, which is why this answer is tempting. Accepting it as the cause without excluding infection is how chlamydia is missed in exactly the group most likely to have it and most likely to suffer tubal damage from it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

options.text: Perform cervical screening today, since a test more than twelve months old is unreliable
options.rationale: Screening under the renewed program is five yearly after a negative result, so hers is not due and repeating it early does not change her management. A screening test is also not the right instrument for investigating a symptom, which is assessed on its own merits. (Source: National Cervical Screening Program: Guidelines)

options.text: Change to a pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinyloestradiol to settle the bleeding
options.rationale: Breakthrough bleeding in the first months of a new pill often settles, and changing the formulation is a reasonable step once other causes have been excluded. Reducing the oestrogen dose usually makes breakthrough bleeding worse rather than better, and it does nothing about an untreated infection. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Combined oral contraception)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Combined oral contraception

explanation.summary: A symmetrical ring of red velvety tissue around the external os is columnar epithelium sitting on the outer cervix, which is a normal variant common in young women, in pregnancy and on oestrogen containing contraception. It bleeds on contact and is therefore an appealing explanation for postcoital bleeding, but it is present in many women without symptoms, so it is a finding rather than a diagnosis. The important differential in a sexually active woman with a new partner is chlamydial or gonococcal cervicitis, which commonly causes intermenstrual and postcoital bleeding with no discharge and no pain. Swabs are taken before the bleeding is attributed to the appearance, and treatment with partner notification follows a positive result. Colposcopy is reserved for a suspicious lesion, an abnormal screening result, or persistent bleeding once infection has been excluded and treated.
key_points: Columnar epithelium on the outer cervix is a normal variant that bleeds on contact.
It is present in many asymptomatic women, so it is a finding rather than a diagnosis.
Chlamydial cervicitis commonly causes contact bleeding with no discharge or pain.
A negative human papillomavirus result makes significant cervical disease unlikely.
Persistent bleeding after infection is excluded and treated warrants colposcopy.
explanation.pearls: Never let a visible ectropion close the consultation in a woman under thirty with a new partner, because chlamydia causes the same contact bleeding, is usually silent otherwise, and the tubal damage it causes is what she presents with in ten years time.

subtopic_detail: the oral cover required when a depot antipsychotic is started, which differs between preparations
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 28 year old man with schizophrenia who has had two relapses in three years, each following a period of stopping his tablets. He has been well for four months on oral aripiprazole 15 mg daily and has agreed to move to a monthly injection.

He tolerates the oral medicine without akathisia, sedation or movement problems, and his most recent metabolic screen was unremarkable. He lives with his parents, who prompt him with tablets, and he is returning to study next month. The first injection of aripiprazole 400 mg is given today in the clinic. He asks whether he can stop the tablets now that he has had the injection.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 122/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No rigidity, tremor or abnormal involuntary movements, weight stable over four months, injection site normal
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose, lipids, full blood count, electrolytes and liver function all within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Aripiprazole 15 mg orally daily, aripiprazole 400 mg intramuscular given today

lead_in: What should you advise about his oral medicine?

options.text: Halve the oral dose today and stop it after the second injection next month
options.rationale: Halving the dose during the period of lowest injectable concentration is the worst of both options, giving inadequate cover for a fortnight while still requiring tablets. The oral dose is maintained in full and then stopped, not tapered. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

options.text: Continue the oral dose for three weeks, as required with the risperidone injection
options.rationale: Three weeks of oral cover is exactly right for the risperidone long acting injection, which releases nothing for about three weeks after administration. Applying that interval here gives a week of unnecessary double treatment and shows the cover period belongs to the preparation rather than to depots as a class. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

options.text: Stop the oral dose today because the injection provides immediate therapeutic cover
options.rationale: One long acting preparation is designed to be started without oral cover by giving two loading injections a week apart, which is why this belief is common on the wards. That approach belongs to the paliperidone preparation and cannot be transferred to an agent that reaches therapeutic levels slowly. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

options.text: Continue the oral dose for fourteen days after this injection and then stop it
options.rationale: This preparation takes several weeks to reach therapeutic plasma concentrations after a single injection, so fourteen days of continued oral treatment covers the gap and is built into the product information. Stopping earlier leaves him subtherapeutic during the very period the change was made to protect. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antipsychotics)

options.text: Continue the oral dose indefinitely because injections alone rarely maintain remission
options.rationale: Long acting injections maintain plasma concentrations at least as well as oral treatment and reduce relapse driven by missed doses, which is the problem he has had twice. Permanent dual treatment doubles his exposure and defeats the purpose of the change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Schizophrenia)

explanation.summary: Long acting injectable antipsychotics differ from each other in how quickly they reach therapeutic plasma concentrations, and the oral cover required at initiation follows the individual preparation rather than any general rule. Aripiprazole given monthly requires fourteen days of continued oral aripiprazole after the first injection. The risperidone injection requires about three weeks of oral cover because it releases almost no drug for the first weeks. Paliperidone palmitate requires none at all, because the regimen uses a loading dose on day one and a second dose on day eight to reach therapeutic levels directly. Getting this wrong produces a relapse a few weeks after a change that was made specifically to prevent one.
key_points: Oral cover at initiation is determined by the individual preparation, not by depots as a class.
Monthly aripiprazole requires fourteen days of continued oral aripiprazole.
The risperidone long acting injection requires about three weeks of oral cover.
Paliperidone palmitate requires no oral cover because of its day one and day eight loading.
Long acting injections reduce relapse driven by missed doses.
explanation.pearls: Write the stop date for the tablets on the prescription and in the clinic letter when you give the first injection, because the relapse that follows a depot change almost always happens in the first month and almost always traces back to the tablets being stopped on the day of the injection.

subtopic_detail: the rebound that follows stopping a monoclonal antiresorptive without replacing it
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 68 year old woman who has had six monthly denosumab injections for three years after a wrist fracture. She tells you she has decided to stop because she dislikes injections and feels her bones must be stronger now. Her last injection was five months ago and the next is due in four weeks.

She has had no new fractures and no back pain. Her repeat bone density scan last month showed a lumbar spine T score improved from minus 2.9 to minus 2.2. Her renal function is normal, her corrected calcium is normal and her vitamin D is adequate on supplementation. She has no history of dental problems and no upper gastrointestinal symptoms, and she takes no corticosteroids.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No spinal tenderness, height unchanged from two years ago, no kyphosis, dentition in good condition
data_table.Investigations: Corrected calcium 2.35 mmol/L (2.10-2.60), creatinine 68 micromol/L (45-90), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60, 25 hydroxyvitamin D 78 nmol/L (above 50), lumbar spine T score minus 2.2
data_table.Medications: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneously six monthly, colecalciferol 1000 units daily, calcium from diet

lead_in: What should you recommend?

options.text: Stop now and start teriparatide instead, given her improved bone density result
options.rationale: Teriparatide is an anabolic agent reserved for severe osteoporosis with fractures despite antiresorptive treatment, and it is not funded in this situation. Giving it after this drug also produces a transient fall in bone density at the hip, which makes it a poor choice for the sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Start an oral bisphosphonate to begin when the next injection would have been due
options.rationale: Stopping this drug without replacement produces a rebound in bone turnover that returns density to baseline within a year and causes multiple vertebral fractures in a substantial minority of women. Following it with a bisphosphonate started around the time the next dose was due preserves the gain she has made and is the specific measure that prevents the rebound. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Extend the dosing interval to twelve monthly as a compromise she may find acceptable
options.rationale: The suppression of bone turnover wanes markedly by about seven months after a dose, so a twelve monthly interval delivers a rebound period twice a year rather than avoiding one. Delay of more than a month beyond the due date is itself associated with vertebral fracture. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Denosumab)

options.text: Continue the injections indefinitely because stopping is never appropriate with this drug
options.rationale: Long term continuation is a reasonable plan for many patients and avoids the problem altogether, but it is not the only safe option and it disregards a clear preference she has expressed. The requirement is not that she continues forever, only that she does not stop without cover. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

options.text: Agree to stop and repeat her bone density scan in two years to check for any loss
options.rationale: Simply stopping is safe with the bisphosphonates, where the drug remains bound to bone for years and a drug holiday is a recognised strategy. It is unsafe with this agent, whose effect disappears entirely once dosing ceases, and a scan in two years would document the fractures rather than prevent them. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Osteoporosis)

explanation.summary: Denosumab inhibits osteoclast formation but is not incorporated into bone, so its effect depends entirely on continued dosing and disappears once it stops. Cessation is followed by a sharp rebound in bone turnover, loss of the accumulated density within about twelve months, and multiple vertebral fractures in a meaningful proportion of patients, often occurring together. This distinguishes it sharply from the bisphosphonates, which bind to bone mineral and continue to act for years after the last dose, allowing a planned drug holiday. Anyone stopping denosumab therefore needs an antiresorptive to follow it, usually an oral bisphosphonate or a zoledronic acid infusion, started around the time the next injection would have fallen due. Even routine delays of more than a month beyond the due date are associated with increased vertebral fracture risk.
key_points: Denosumab is not incorporated into bone and its effect stops when dosing stops.
Cessation causes rebound turnover and multiple vertebral fractures in a substantial minority.
Bisphosphonates bind to bone and permit a planned drug holiday, which this drug does not.
Follow on antiresorptive treatment is started around the time the next dose was due.
Delaying a dose beyond about a month is itself associated with vertebral fracture.
explanation.pearls: Treat a missed denosumab appointment as urgent rather than routine, because the fractures that follow cluster in the months after a delayed or abandoned dose and typically present as several vertebral fractures at once in a woman who had been doing well.

subtopic_detail: deciding whether repeated nosebleeds in a well child need a bleeding disorder workup
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 7 year old boy who has had about eight nosebleeds in the past two months. His mother says each one comes from the right nostril, starts while he is watching television or soon after he has been picking his nose, and stops within ten minutes when she pinches the bridge of his nose for him.

He has never bled from the gums or into a joint, has never bruised without an injury, and had a tonsillectomy at five without excessive bleeding. No relative has a bleeding problem or has needed transfusion after surgery. The family has recently started using ducted heating through the winter. On examination the anterior part of the right septum is crusted and reddened, and the rest of the examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Crusted excoriated area on the anterior right nasal septum, no petechiae, no bruises beyond both shins, no lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Correct the pressure technique and prescribe an antiseptic nasal ointment for two weeks
options.rationale: Bleeding from one nostril in a well child with a visible excoriated area on the anterior septum is local in origin, and treatment is directed at the mucosa and at the technique. Pressure belongs on the soft part of the nose rather than the bony bridge, and an antiseptic ointment reduces crusting and staphylococcal colonisation, which shortens the run of bleeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Refer to an ear nose and throat surgeon for chemical cautery of the septal vessels
options.rationale: Cautery is reserved for bleeding that continues despite mucosal treatment and correct first aid, and it carries a risk of septal injury when the mucosa is already excoriated. It is a second line step rather than the opening move in a child having short self limiting bleeds. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Advise a saline spray alone and review him again only if the bleeding worsens
options.rationale: Saline addresses dryness from heated indoor air and is a reasonable adjunct, but on its own it leaves the colonised excoriated area untreated and the family still pinching the wrong part of the nose. The technique correction is the part of this consultation that most reliably shortens each episode. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Request a full blood count, coagulation profile and von Willebrand factor studies
options.rationale: A haemostatic workup is indicated when bleeding comes from both nostrils, lasts beyond about ten minutes despite correct pressure, involves other sites, or where surgery or family history suggests a disorder. None of those apply, and he bled normally at tonsillectomy, which is a substantial haemostatic challenge. (Source: RCH CPG: Epistaxis)

options.text: Arrange nasal endoscopy to exclude a mass in the posterior nasal space
options.rationale: Endoscopy is warranted for unilateral obstruction, foul discharge or profuse posterior bleeding, particularly in an adolescent boy where a vascular nasal tumour is a consideration. Short anterior bleeds with a visible septal cause in a 7 year old do not raise that possibility. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Epistaxis)

explanation.summary: Most childhood nosebleeds arise from the anterior septum, where a superficial vascular plexus sits close to the surface and is easily damaged by picking and by dry heated air. The features that separate this local pattern from a bleeding disorder are the single nostril, the short duration with pressure, the absence of bleeding at other sites, and an uneventful tonsillectomy. Management is mucosal treatment plus correcting the first aid, because families very commonly pinch the bony bridge, which does not compress the bleeding point. Antiseptic ointment reduces crusting and colonisation and is a reasonable first line in Australian practice. Cautery and haematological investigation both sit downstream of this step.
key_points: The anterior septum is the source of the great majority of childhood nosebleeds.
Pressure must be applied to the soft part of the nose, not the bony bridge.
Bleeding from both nostrils or at other sites shifts the assessment toward a haemostatic disorder.
Normal haemostasis at tonsillectomy is strong evidence against an inherited bleeding disorder.
Unilateral obstruction with profuse bleeding in an adolescent boy warrants imaging and endoscopy.
explanation.pearls: Ask the parent to demonstrate how they hold the nose, because most families compress the bony bridge where no bleeding vessel lies, and ten minutes of correctly applied pressure to the soft part settles nearly all anterior bleeds without any prescription at all.

subtopic_detail: whether immunoglobulin is owed for first trimester bleeding with a viable intrauterine pregnancy
stem:
You are the resident in the early pregnancy assessment service seeing a 29 year old woman in her first pregnancy at 9 weeks and 2 days with two days of light red spotting that needed a liner but not a pad. The bleeding has now stopped.

She has mild lower abdominal cramping that she rates 2 out of 10, no shoulder tip pain, no dizziness and no passage of tissue. She has had no procedures in this pregnancy, no trauma and no abdominal injury. Her booking bloods show blood group O rhesus D negative with a negative antibody screen. Transvaginal ultrasound today shows a single intrauterine gestation with a crown rump length matching dates, cardiac activity present, and a small subchorionic haematoma. Her cervix is closed on speculum examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 112/68 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Abdomen soft with mild suprapubic tenderness, cervical os closed, minimal old blood in the vault, no adnexal mass
data_table.Investigations: Blood group O rhesus D negative, antibody screen negative, haemoglobin 128 g/L (115-155), ultrasound viable intrauterine pregnancy with small subchorionic haematoma

lead_in: What should you do about her rhesus status?

options.text: Send a Kleihauer test and give immunoglobulin only if fetomaternal haemorrhage is shown
options.rationale: Quantifying fetomaternal haemorrhage guides the dose after a sensitising event from 20 weeks, such as abdominal trauma or antepartum haemorrhage. Before 12 weeks the foetal red cell volume is below the detection threshold of the test, so a negative result carries no reassurance and no decision rests on it. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Give 250 IU of anti D immunoglobulin today because she has bled in this pregnancy
options.rationale: That dose is the correct one for a sensitising event before 12 weeks, and such events include ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, termination, miscarriage with instrumentation and chorionic villus sampling. Threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy at this gestation is specifically not on that list. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Give 625 IU of anti D immunoglobulin today and repeat the antibody screen in six weeks
options.rationale: The larger dose belongs to sensitising events from 12 weeks onward, so it is both the wrong indication and the wrong dose here. Repeating the antibody screen shortly after giving immunoglobulin is also unhelpful because passively acquired anti D cannot be distinguished from immune anti D on a routine screen. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

options.text: Arrange cell free foetal DNA typing to establish the foetal rhesus group before deciding
options.rationale: Foetal blood group typing from maternal plasma is used in some settings to avoid unnecessary prophylaxis, but it is not part of routine Australian care and is not reliable this early in pregnancy. It would also delay a decision that does not need the information. (Source: Lifeblood: Anti D in pregnancy)

options.text: Give no immunoglobulin now and arrange the routine dose in the third trimester
options.rationale: Prophylaxis is not recommended for threatened miscarriage below 12 weeks where the pregnancy is intrauterine and viable, because the fetomaternal haemorrhage at this gestation is too small to sensitise and the foetal red cell mass is minimal. She remains on the routine pathway, which is a dose at 28 weeks and again at 34 weeks, plus a dose after birth if the baby is rhesus D positive. (Source: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

explanation.summary: Rhesus D immunoglobulin prevents maternal sensitisation by clearing foetal red cells before the immune system responds to them, so the indication depends on whether enough foetal red cells could plausibly have entered the maternal circulation. Before 12 weeks the foetal red cell mass is tiny, and threatened miscarriage with a viable intrauterine pregnancy is not considered a sensitising event in Australian guidance. Events before 12 weeks that do warrant the 250 IU dose are ectopic pregnancy, molar pregnancy, termination, miscarriage involving instrumentation and chorionic villus sampling. From 12 weeks the dose rises to 625 IU, and from 20 weeks a Kleihauer test is used to determine whether additional doses are needed. This woman continues on routine antenatal prophylaxis at 28 and 34 weeks with a postnatal dose if the baby types as rhesus D positive.
key_points: Threatened miscarriage below 12 weeks with a viable intrauterine pregnancy does not require prophylaxis.
Sensitising events before 12 weeks warrant 250 IU, and from 12 weeks 625 IU.
Ectopic and molar pregnancy, termination and chorionic villus sampling are sensitising at any gestation.
Kleihauer testing guides additional dosing only from 20 weeks.
Routine antenatal prophylaxis is given at 28 and 34 weeks with a postnatal dose if the baby is positive.
explanation.pearls: Anchor on 12 weeks and on whether the uterus was instrumented: bleeding alone before 12 weeks in a viable intrauterine pregnancy earns no immunoglobulin, but the same bleeding after a curette or a chorionic villus sample earns 250 IU within 72 hours.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Guidelines for the use of Rh(D) immunoglobulin

subtopic_detail: the interval required before an irreversible enzyme inhibitor can follow an antidepressant with an active metabolite
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar seeing a 44 year old woman with severe depression that has not responded to three adequate antidepressant trials. Your consultant has decided to move her to phenelzine and has asked you to organise the change.

She is currently taking fluoxetine 40 mg daily, which she has been on for eleven weeks with no benefit. She has no psychotic symptoms, is not suicidal, and lives with her husband who is supportive. She has no cardiac or renal disease, takes no other prescribed medicine and uses no over the counter preparations or herbal supplements. She has already been counselled about the dietary restrictions that go with the new medicine and is keen to start as soon as possible.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No tremor, no clonus, no hyperreflexia, no rigidity, mental state shows low mood with reactive affect and no psychosis
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Fluoxetine 40 mg orally daily

lead_in: How should the change be made?

options.text: Switch to a two week course of sertraline first and then allow a two week washout
options.rationale: Bridging through a shorter acting agent sounds appealing and would shorten the final washout on paper. It requires the fluoxetine metabolite to be gone before the sertraline is stopped, which it will not be, so the total wait is no shorter and the patient takes an extra medicine for no reason. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Switching antidepressants)

options.text: Cross taper the two medicines over ten days to avoid a period without treatment
options.rationale: Cross tapering is standard practice between most antidepressants and avoids both discontinuation symptoms and a treatment gap. It is specifically contraindicated with this class, because any overlap between a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor risks life threatening serotonin toxicity. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Switching antidepressants)

options.text: Stop the fluoxetine and wait five weeks before the first dose of the new medicine
options.rationale: Fluoxetine and its active metabolite have half lives measured in days to weeks, so serotonergic activity persists long after the last tablet and a standard two week gap is not enough. Five weeks allows near complete elimination before an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor is introduced, which is what prevents a severe serotonin toxicity reaction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Stop the fluoxetine and wait two weeks before the first dose of the new medicine
options.rationale: Two weeks is the correct interval after sertraline, citalopram, escitalopram or paroxetine, whose elimination is complete in that time. Applying it to fluoxetine ignores the metabolite that continues to inhibit serotonin reuptake for weeks afterwards. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Halve the fluoxetine for two weeks and then start the new medicine at a low dose
options.rationale: Reducing the dose shortens neither the half life nor the elimination time of the active metabolite, so the overlap risk is unchanged. A low starting dose of the new agent does not protect against a reaction that is driven by the combination rather than the dose. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Combining a serotonin reuptake inhibitor with an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor can cause severe serotonin toxicity, with hyperthermia, rigidity, clonus and autonomic instability, which is why a complete washout is required rather than a cross taper. The length of the washout is set by the elimination of the drug and any active metabolites. Fluoxetine is the outlier among the selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors because its metabolite has a half life of one to two weeks, so five weeks are needed after the last dose, against two weeks for the other agents in the class. Going the other way, two weeks are required after stopping an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor before a serotonergic drug is introduced, because new enzyme must be synthesised. Dose reduction does not substitute for time, since half life is unchanged by dose.
key_points: Serotonin toxicity presents with hyperthermia, clonus, hyperreflexia and autonomic instability.
A cross taper is never used between a serotonin reuptake inhibitor and an irreversible monoamine oxidase inhibitor.
Fluoxetine requires a five week washout because of its long acting metabolite.
Other selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors require two weeks.
Two weeks are needed after stopping the inhibitor before any serotonergic drug is started.
explanation.pearls: Fluoxetine is the one antidepressant where the washout is measured in weeks rather than days, so before any switch involving it, check whether the incoming drug is serotonergic and count five weeks from the last tablet, not from the last clinic visit.

subtopic_detail: the fourth agent to add once three classes at maximum tolerated dose have not reached target
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 58 year old man whose blood pressure remains above target despite three medicines. His home readings over the past fortnight average 158/94 mmHg, and his clinic reading today is 162/96 mmHg in both arms.

He takes perindopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily and indapamide 2.5 mg daily, all at maximum tolerated doses, and his dispensing history confirms he collects all three every month. He does not use non steroidal anti inflammatories, decongestants or liquorice, drinks two standard drinks a week and does not snore or have witnessed apnoeas. His renal artery imaging last year was normal and his aldosterone to renin ratio was not suggestive of primary aldosteronism. His potassium today is 3.9 mmol/L and his estimated glomerular filtration rate is above 60.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 162/96 mmHg both arms, pulse rate 72/min regular, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 29, no radiofemoral delay, no abdominal bruit, fundoscopy shows arteriovenous nipping without haemorrhage
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 3.9 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 140 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 82 micromol/L (60-110), estimated glomerular filtration rate above 60, aldosterone to renin ratio not elevated
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 10 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg daily

lead_in: Which medicine should you add next?

options.text: Spironolactone 25 mg daily with electrolytes rechecked within one to two weeks
options.rationale: In resistant hypertension where adherence is confirmed and secondary causes have been addressed, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist lowers blood pressure more than a beta blocker or an alpha blocker added at the same point. His potassium at 3.9 mmol/L and preserved renal function make it safe to start, with a check within a fortnight because the combination with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor raises the risk of hyperkalaemia. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

options.text: Candesartan 16 mg daily in addition to his current angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor
options.rationale: Combining an angiotensin receptor blocker with an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor gives little additional blood pressure reduction while significantly increasing hyperkalaemia, acute kidney injury and hypotension. This combination is avoided in current practice. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypertension)

options.text: Prazosin 1 mg twice daily, increasing the dose according to his tolerance
options.rationale: An alpha blocker is an accepted later line option and is useful where prostatic symptoms coexist. It is less effective than the preferred agent at this step and causes postural hypotension, so it sits behind it in the sequence. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

options.text: Bisoprolol 5 mg daily, titrating upward according to his heart rate response
options.rationale: A beta blocker is a reasonable fourth agent where there is a compelling indication such as angina, prior myocardial infarction or heart failure, and it remains an option if the preferred agent cannot be used. Compared head to head at this point in the sequence it produces a smaller blood pressure reduction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Resistant hypertension)

options.text: Substitute hydrochlorothiazide for the indapamide before adding any further agent
options.rationale: Swapping between thiazide type diuretics is worth considering when the current one is poorly tolerated, and indapamide is at least as effective as hydrochlorothiazide. Exchanging one for the other adds no blood pressure reduction and delays the step that will. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypertension)

explanation.summary: Resistant hypertension is defined as blood pressure above target despite three agents from different classes, including a diuretic, at maximum tolerated doses. Before adding a fourth drug, three things must be established: that the readings are real rather than white coat, that the patient is actually taking the medicines, and that contributing causes such as non steroidal anti inflammatories, alcohol, sleep apnoea, renal artery disease and primary aldosteronism have been considered. Once that groundwork is done, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist is the fourth agent with the best evidence, outperforming both a beta blocker and an alpha blocker when tested directly in this population. The main hazard is hyperkalaemia, particularly alongside an angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitor or in renal impairment, so electrolytes are checked within one to two weeks of starting and after any dose increase. A starting potassium at the lower end of normal, as here, makes the choice comfortable.
key_points: Resistant hypertension means above target on three agents including a diuretic.
Confirm adherence and exclude contributing causes before adding a fourth drug.
A mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist outperforms a beta blocker or alpha blocker at this step.
Hyperkalaemia is the main hazard, so electrolytes are checked within one to two weeks.
Combining an angiotensin receptor blocker with a converting enzyme inhibitor is avoided.
explanation.pearls: Check the dispensing history before calling any hypertension resistant, because roughly half the patients referred for resistant hypertension are not taking what is on the list, and adding a fourth drug to a regimen nobody is taking achieves nothing but hyperkalaemia risk.

subtopic_detail: anterior knee pain in a growing athlete where the site of tenderness decides the management
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 13 year old boy who plays basketball four times a week and has had three months of pain at the front of his right knee. He says it is worst going up stairs and during jumping drills, settles within a day of rest, and has never woken him at night.

He has grown 9 cm in the past year. He has not had fevers, weight loss or night sweats, and the knee has never given way, locked or swollen. On examination he is tender over a prominent bony lump below the kneecap, the joint line is not tender, and there is no effusion. Extending the knee against resistance reproduces his pain, and hip rotation is full and painless on both sides.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Prominent tender tibial tubercle on the right, no joint effusion, no joint line tenderness, full painless internal rotation of both hips, no warmth or erythema
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Refer to orthopaedics for consideration of excision of the bony prominence
options.rationale: Surgery to remove a residual ossicle is confined to skeletally mature patients whose symptoms have persisted well beyond the end of growth despite full conservative treatment. Operating during the growth spurt risks the tubercle and is never the first response. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

options.text: Request plain radiographs of the knee in two planes before starting any treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated for night pain, rest pain, systemic symptoms, an effusion or a history of significant trauma, because those raise the possibility of bone tumour or an internal derangement. Focal tenderness over the tubercle with pain reproduced by resisted extension is a clinical diagnosis and radiographs add nothing. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

options.text: Inject corticosteroid around the tender prominence and allow return to sport
options.rationale: Corticosteroid placed near a tendon insertion weakens the collagen and risks avulsion of the apophysis, which is precisely the structure already under traction stress. There is no role for injection in this condition at any stage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children

options.text: Request pelvic radiographs including frog lateral views of both hips today
options.rationale: Referred pain from a slipped upper femoral epiphysis genuinely can present as knee pain in this age group, which is why hip rotation must be examined in every adolescent with knee pain. Full and painless internal rotation of both hips makes that diagnosis very unlikely here. (Source: RCH CPG: Limp)

options.text: Advise relative rest with a quadriceps stretching programme and simple analgesia
options.rationale: Traction apophysitis at the tibial tubercle is a self limiting overuse condition of the growth spurt, and load modification with a stretching programme addresses the tight extensor mechanism that drives it. Complete withdrawal from sport is neither necessary nor helpful, so activity is reduced to a level that does not provoke pain while flexibility improves. (Source: RCH CPG: Knee pain)

explanation.summary: Anterior knee pain in a rapidly growing adolescent athlete, with tenderness localised to the tibial tubercle and pain reproduced by resisted knee extension, is traction apophysitis at the patellar tendon insertion. The absence of night pain, rest pain, systemic features and effusion removes the presentations that require imaging, and full painless hip rotation removes the referred pain from a slipped epiphysis that must always be considered. Treatment is load modification rather than cessation of sport, combined with stretching of the quadriceps and hamstrings, because reduced flexibility during the growth spurt increases traction on the apophysis. The condition resolves as the apophysis fuses, and families need to be told the prominence itself will remain. Persisting symptoms after skeletal maturity are the only situation in which surgery is discussed.
key_points: Tenderness confined to the tibial tubercle with a normal joint line indicates apophysitis, not internal derangement.
Every adolescent with knee pain needs hip rotation examined to exclude referred pain.
Night pain, rest pain or systemic symptoms mandate radiographs to exclude bone tumour.
Load is reduced to a pain tolerable level rather than stopped altogether.
The bony prominence persists after symptoms resolve and does not indicate treatment failure.
explanation.pearls: Tell the family at the first visit that the lump is permanent even though the pain is not, because otherwise they return repeatedly for the unchanged prominence and are offered imaging that was never indicated.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Musculoskeletal pain in children

subtopic_detail: counselling on mode of birth after a repaired anal sphincter injury in a woman with no continence symptoms
stem:
You are the registrar in the antenatal clinic seeing a 31 year old woman at 30 weeks in her second pregnancy. Her first birth was a forceps delivery with a third degree tear repaired in theatre by a consultant, and she asks whether she should have a caesarean this time.

She has no leakage of wind or stool, no urgency and no soiling, and she says her bowel control feels the same as it did before her first baby. She had physiotherapy for six months afterwards and completes pelvic floor exercises most days. Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound arranged by the perineal clinic eighteen months ago were reported as normal. This pregnancy has been uncomplicated, the foetus is cephalic with growth on the 55th centile, and the estimated foetal weight is similar to her first baby.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symphysis fundal height 30 cm, cephalic presentation, foetal heart rate 142/min, perineum well healed with no scarring tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound normal eighteen months ago, growth scan estimated foetal weight on the 55th centile

lead_in: What would you advise her about mode of birth?

options.text: Support a planned vaginal birth, noting her normal symptoms and normal investigations
options.rationale: A woman who has no continence symptoms and normal anorectal testing after a repaired sphincter injury has a low risk of lasting deterioration and can be supported toward vaginal birth. The recurrence risk of a further sphincter injury is around five to seven per cent, which does not by itself justify abdominal surgery in an asymptomatic woman. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Recommend vaginal birth with a routine episiotomy performed to protect the sphincter
options.rationale: Routine episiotomy does not prevent sphincter injury and midline episiotomy increases it, so it is performed for a clinical indication rather than as a prophylactic measure. Perineal protection during crowning and a warm compress have better evidence. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Plan vaginal birth but avoid instrumental delivery by proceeding directly to caesarean
options.rationale: Forceps carries a higher risk of sphincter injury than vacuum, so the operator can reasonably prefer vacuum if instrumental birth becomes necessary. Committing in advance to abdominal delivery rather than an assisted vaginal birth removes a safe option and increases the overall operative rate. (Source: RANZCOG: Instrumental vaginal birth)

options.text: Repeat the anorectal manometry and endoanal ultrasound before making any recommendation
options.rationale: Repeat testing is worthwhile where symptoms have developed or where the earlier studies were equivocal, since the result would then change the recommendation. With normal studies and unchanged symptoms, repeating them delays the discussion without altering it. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

options.text: Recommend an elective caesarean because any previous sphincter injury makes it safer
options.rationale: Caesarean is recommended for women who remain symptomatic or who have abnormal endoanal ultrasound or manometry, because a further vaginal birth can convert compensated function into frank incontinence. Applying it to every woman with a previous tear exposes a large number to operative risk for no measurable gain. (Source: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

explanation.summary: The decision after a repaired anal sphincter injury turns on current function rather than on the fact of the previous tear. A woman with no incontinence, no urgency and normal endoanal ultrasound and manometry has adequate reserve, and the recurrence risk of about five to seven per cent does not outweigh the risks of planned abdominal delivery. Caesarean is recommended where symptoms persist or where testing shows a residual sphincter defect or low pressures, because a further vaginal birth can decompensate a sphincter that is only just coping. Routine episiotomy is not protective and midline episiotomy makes injury more likely, so intrapartum care focuses on controlled delivery of the head and perineal support. If an instrumental birth becomes necessary, vacuum carries a lower risk of sphincter injury than forceps.
key_points: Current continence and anorectal testing, not the previous tear itself, drive the recommendation.
Recurrence risk of sphincter injury is approximately five to seven per cent.
Persistent symptoms or an abnormal study shift the recommendation toward caesarean.
Routine episiotomy does not protect the sphincter and midline episiotomy increases injury.
Vacuum extraction carries a lower sphincter injury risk than forceps.
explanation.pearls: Ask specifically about leakage of flatus rather than of stool, because women rarely volunteer it and it is the symptom that most often identifies the compensated sphincter that will decompensate after a second vaginal birth.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Third and fourth degree perineal tears

subtopic_detail: the monitoring schedule that must be arranged before a particular antidepressant is dispensed
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 38 year old man with a first episode of moderate depression whose main complaints are early waking and daytime fatigue. He has previously stopped two antidepressants because of sexual dysfunction and asks specifically about agomelatine, which a colleague at work takes.

He drinks two standard drinks most evenings and has no history of hepatitis, jaundice or alcohol related liver disease. He takes no other medication, has no known allergies and does not use recreational drugs. His weight is stable and his examination is unremarkable. He is engaged with a psychologist and is not suicidal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: No jaundice, no hepatomegaly, no stigmata of chronic liver disease, body mass index 25
data_table.Investigations: No blood tests performed to date
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What must you arrange if you prescribe this medicine?

options.text: No specific monitoring, with review at two weeks to assess response and tolerability
options.rationale: Early review at two weeks is appropriate for any newly started antidepressant and should happen here as well. It is not sufficient on its own for this drug, because hepatic injury is usually asymptomatic until it is advanced and is detected only by scheduled blood tests. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Liver function tests before starting and again at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks
options.rationale: This drug causes dose related transaminase rises and rare cases of hepatic failure, so a baseline is taken before the first tablet and the schedule of repeats covers the period in which injury appears. Treatment is not started when transaminases are above three times the upper limit of normal, and it is stopped if they rise to that level on treatment. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: A full blood count before starting and weekly for the first eighteen weeks of treatment
options.rationale: Weekly haematological monitoring of that intensity belongs to clozapine, where agranulocytosis risk is concentrated in the first months. No antidepressant requires this schedule. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Depression)

options.text: Serum sodium before starting and again at two weeks, then every three months
options.rationale: Sodium monitoring in the early weeks belongs with the serotonin reuptake inhibitors and venlafaxine in older patients, where hyponatraemia from inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion is the recognised early risk. It is not the monitoring requirement that distinguishes this drug. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: An electrocardiogram before starting and again once the maintenance dose is reached
options.rationale: Baseline and follow up electrocardiography is the requirement for citalopram at higher doses and for antipsychotics that prolong the QT interval. This agent has no meaningful effect on cardiac conduction. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

explanation.summary: Agomelatine is an antidepressant acting at melatonergic receptors with additional serotonin antagonism, and it is chosen partly because it is not associated with sexual dysfunction or weight gain. Its distinguishing safety issue is hepatotoxicity, ranging from asymptomatic transaminase elevation to rare hepatic failure, and this drives a mandatory monitoring schedule. Liver function is checked before the first dose and again at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks, and after any dose increase. Treatment is not started if transaminases exceed three times the upper limit of normal, and it is ceased if they reach that threshold during treatment or if the patient develops jaundice, dark urine or right upper quadrant pain. Regular alcohol intake and other hepatotoxic drugs increase the risk and are worth quantifying before prescribing.
key_points: Hepatotoxicity is the distinguishing safety concern with this drug.
Liver function is checked at baseline and at three, six, twelve and twenty four weeks.
Transaminases above three times the upper limit of normal preclude starting or continuing.
It is not associated with sexual dysfunction or weight gain, which is why patients request it.
Hyponatraemia monitoring belongs with serotonin reuptake inhibitors and venlafaxine, not here.
explanation.pearls: Order the baseline liver function test before writing the script rather than with it, because the drug should not be started at all when transaminases exceed three times the upper limit of normal, and a result that arrives after the first week has already missed that decision.

subtopic_detail: committing an asymptomatic patient to lifelong replacement on the strength of a single abnormal result
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 41 year old woman who had thyroid function tested by an after hours service three weeks ago when she attended with a viral illness and fatigue. She feels completely well now and has come for the result.

Her thyroid stimulating hormone is 11.4 mIU/L with a free thyroxine of 14 pmol/L. She has no cold intolerance, constipation, weight change, hair loss or menstrual change, and her energy has returned to normal since the illness settled. She is not pregnant, is not trying to conceive and uses an intrauterine device. She takes no amiodarone, lithium or iodine containing preparation and has had no neck surgery or radiation. Her pulse is 68 beats per minute and there is no goitre or nodule palpable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 116/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No goitre or palpable nodule, no periorbital puffiness, reflexes normal with normal relaxation phase, no dry skin
data_table.Investigations: Thyroid stimulating hormone 11.4 mIU/L (0.4-4.0), free thyroxine 14 pmol/L (10-20), full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Start thyroxine 50 micrograms daily now and recheck the thyroid function in eight weeks
options.rationale: Persistent elevation above 10 mIU/L is an accepted indication to treat, so this is the right destination if the result is confirmed. Starting on a single sample taken during an acute illness commits an asymptomatic woman to lifelong medicine on a result that may well normalise by itself. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Arrange thyroid ultrasound to look for the structural cause of the abnormal result
options.rationale: Ultrasound assesses a palpable nodule or goitre and does not contribute to the assessment of thyroid function, since the biochemistry and antibodies establish the diagnosis. She has a normal neck on examination. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Repeat the thyroid function tests in six to eight weeks with thyroid peroxidase antibodies
options.rationale: A raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine resolves spontaneously in up to a third of people, particularly when the sample was taken during or shortly after an acute illness, which is what happened here. Confirming that the elevation persists before starting lifelong replacement is the point of the repeat, and the antibody result predicts who will progress to overt disease and therefore how closely to follow her. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Reassure her that she is well and repeat the thyroid function only if symptoms appear
options.rationale: Waiting for symptoms is appropriate for a mildly raised result in the range up to about 7 mIU/L in an older person, where the finding often reflects normal ageing. At this level the chance of progression to overt disease is considerably higher, so the result needs following up rather than discarding. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Thyroid disorders)

options.text: Measure free triiodothyronine now to establish whether her thyroid function is adequate
options.rationale: Free triiodothyronine is useful in suspected thyrotoxicosis, where it can be raised while thyroxine remains normal. It stays within range until hypothyroidism is far advanced and adds nothing to the assessment of an underactive gland. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Thyroid hormones)

explanation.summary: Subclinical hypothyroidism is a biochemical diagnosis defined by a raised thyroid stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine, and it is common enough that the first question is always whether the result is real and persistent. Up to a third of elevations resolve spontaneously, and acute illness in particular disturbs the axis, so a single abnormal sample taken during a viral illness cannot support a decision about lifelong treatment. The repeat is taken after six to eight weeks, alongside thyroid peroxidase antibodies, which identify autoimmune disease and predict progression to overt hypothyroidism. If the elevation persists above 10 mIU/L, treatment is generally offered even without symptoms. Different thresholds apply in pregnancy or when conception is planned, where treatment is started at lower levels and sooner.
key_points: Subclinical hypothyroidism means a raised stimulating hormone with a normal free thyroxine.
Up to a third of elevations resolve spontaneously, particularly after acute illness.
Confirm persistence at six to eight weeks before committing to lifelong replacement.
Thyroid peroxidase antibodies predict progression to overt hypothyroidism.
Pregnancy and planned conception use lower thresholds and earlier treatment.
explanation.pearls: Ask why the test was ordered before you act on it, because a thyroid stimulating hormone measured during an acute illness is the commonest reason a well person ends up on thyroxine for life, and the repeat six weeks later is normal surprisingly often.

subtopic_detail: responding to parental refusal of the newborn intramuscular prophylaxis without losing the protection entirely
stem:
You are the resident on the postnatal ward asked to see the parents of a healthy boy born two hours ago at 39 weeks by normal vaginal birth, weighing 3480 g. They have declined the intramuscular vitamin K injection after reading that the dose is far larger than a newborn would receive naturally, and they say they will not consent to an injection under any circumstances.

They are articulate, have asked good questions, and say they will accept anything given by mouth. The mother took no medications in pregnancy, has no liver disease, and plans to breastfeed exclusively. The baby has fed once, has normal tone and colour, and his examination is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 140/min, respiratory rate 46/min, SpO2 98% in air, temperature 36.9 degrees C, blood pressure not indicated
data_table.Examination: Term male infant, normal tone and cry, no bruising or cephalohaematoma, red reflex present bilaterally, femoral pulses palpable
data_table.Investigations: None indicated
data_table.Medications: Maternal medications nil in pregnancy

lead_in: What should you do next?

options.text: Notify child protection services because refusal places the infant at risk of harm
options.rationale: Notification is reserved for refusal of treatment for an established life threatening condition, not for declining prophylaxis where a reasonable alternative is accepted. Escalating at this point damages a relationship these parents have engaged with and would not change the outcome. (Source: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

options.text: Advise the mother to take a daily supplement so that her breastmilk supplies enough
options.rationale: Maternal supplementation raises breastmilk concentrations only modestly and unpredictably, and breastmilk is inherently a poor source, which is why exclusively breastfed infants carry the highest risk of late bleeding. It cannot be relied on as the infant prophylaxis. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

options.text: Offer the three dose oral regimen and document the discussion of the residual bleeding risk
options.rationale: Where an injection is refused, the oral schedule of three doses given at birth, at three to five days and at four weeks is the recognised alternative for a breastfed infant and preserves most of the protection. It is less effective than the single intramuscular dose, particularly against late bleeding, so the discussion and the residual risk are recorded and the parents are told the later doses are essential. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

options.text: Give the injection once the parents have left the room and record it in the notes
options.rationale: Treating a child against an explicit parental refusal without legal authority is an assault and destroys the trust on which every subsequent conversation depends. The strength of the clinical case for the injection does not create consent. (Source: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

options.text: Accept the refusal and arrange close follow up with the child health nurse instead
options.rationale: Surveillance does not prevent bleeding, and late haemorrhagic disease presents as intracranial bleeding without warning signs in a previously well infant. Declining the injection is the parents right, but leaving the infant with no prophylaxis at all when an oral alternative is available is not an equivalent plan. (Source: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K)
source_refs: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K

explanation.summary: Newborn bleeding from vitamin K deficiency has an early form in the first week and a late form at two to twelve weeks that typically presents as intracranial haemorrhage, and the late form is almost confined to exclusively breastfed infants who received no prophylaxis. A single intramuscular dose is the most effective prevention, but when parents refuse it the oral schedule of three doses is the accepted alternative and is markedly better than nothing. Because oral prophylaxis fails more often, especially in infants with unrecognised cholestasis, the later two doses must be arranged explicitly rather than left to chance. Accepting outright refusal, giving the injection covertly and relying on maternal supplementation are all unsafe responses in different ways. The conversation and the residual risk belong in the record.
key_points: Late bleeding occurs at two to twelve weeks and often presents as intracranial haemorrhage.
Exclusively breastfed infants who receive no prophylaxis carry the highest risk.
The oral alternative is three doses, at birth, at three to five days and at four weeks.
Oral prophylaxis fails more often than intramuscular, particularly with undiagnosed cholestasis.
Treating a child over an explicit parental refusal without legal authority is unlawful.
explanation.pearls: When parents accept the oral route, book the four week dose before they leave the ward, because the third dose is the one families forget and it is the dose that covers the window in which late intracranial bleeding actually occurs.

sources.label: NHMRC and Australian Government: Joint statement on vitamin K
RCH CPG: Consent and refusal of treatment

subtopic_detail: setting the timing of birth in twins according to the chorionicity determined in the first trimester
stem:
You are the registrar seeing a 33 year old woman at 32 weeks in a twin pregnancy conceived after in vitro fertilisation with two embryos transferred. She asks when her babies will be born and whether she needs a caesarean.

The dating scan at 12 weeks showed two separate placental masses with a thick dividing membrane and a lambda sign at the base. Growth scans every four weeks have shown both twins tracking on the 40th and 50th centiles with normal umbilical artery Doppler studies and normal liquor volumes. Her blood pressure has been normal throughout, her oral glucose tolerance test was normal, and she has had no bleeding, contractions or ruptured membranes. Twin one is cephalic and twin two is transverse today.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 88/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Uterus large for dates as expected, twin one cephalic, twin two transverse, no uterine tenderness or contractions
data_table.Investigations: Dating scan lambda sign with two placental masses, growth scans both twins on the 40th and 50th centiles, normal umbilical artery Doppler studies, haemoglobin 108 g/L (110-140)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate plan for timing of birth?

options.text: Plan birth at 37 to 38 weeks and decide the mode closer to the time
options.rationale: The lambda sign with two placental masses establishes a dichorionic pregnancy, which does not carry the vascular anastomoses responsible for the sudden losses seen in monochorionic twins, so birth is planned later than in those pregnancies. Beyond 38 weeks the stillbirth risk in dichorionic twins rises, and the presentation of the second twin at 32 weeks does not predict the presentation at birth. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Plan birth at 36 to 37 weeks because of the risk of unexpected loss in twin pregnancy
options.rationale: That earlier window applies to monochorionic diamniotic pregnancies, where shared placental circulation creates a risk of sudden intrauterine death that increases from the late third trimester. Applying it to a dichorionic pregnancy delivers a large number of babies early for a risk they do not carry. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Continue to 40 weeks with twice weekly monitoring as for any uncomplicated pregnancy
options.rationale: Twin pregnancies have a higher stillbirth rate than singletons at every gestation and that rate climbs steeply beyond 38 weeks, which is why expectant management to term plus is not offered. Surveillance does not reliably predict the losses that occur in this window. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Plan an elective caesarean at 34 weeks with corticosteroids because twin two is transverse
options.rationale: The presentation of the second twin at 32 weeks changes frequently and is determined at the time of birth, not now, so it cannot drive the timing. Birth at 34 weeks in an uncomplicated pregnancy imposes substantial prematurity for no indication. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

options.text: Plan birth at 32 to 34 weeks given the low haemoglobin and the twin pregnancy
options.rationale: A haemoglobin of 108 g/L reflects the physiological dilution that is more pronounced in twins, and it is managed with iron studies and replacement rather than by delivery. It is not an indication for preterm birth in a woman with normal growth and Doppler studies. (Source: RANZCOG: Iron deficiency in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Chorionicity determined in the first trimester governs almost every subsequent decision in twin pregnancy, including the frequency of scans and the timing of birth. The lambda sign with two separate placental masses identifies a dichorionic pregnancy, in which each twin has its own placental circulation and the risks of twin to twin transfusion and sudden co twin demise do not apply. Uncomplicated dichorionic twins are therefore delivered at 37 to 38 weeks, while monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered at 36 to 37 weeks and monoamniotic pregnancies considerably earlier. The rationale for not continuing past 38 weeks is the steep rise in stillbirth beyond that gestation rather than any problem in this pregnancy. Mode of birth is decided near term and vaginal birth remains appropriate when the first twin is cephalic, whatever the second twin is doing weeks beforehand.
key_points: The lambda sign with two placental masses indicates dichorionicity.
Uncomplicated dichorionic twins are delivered at 37 to 38 weeks.
Monochorionic diamniotic twins are delivered earlier, at 36 to 37 weeks.
Stillbirth risk in twins rises steeply beyond 38 weeks.
The presentation of the second twin is determined at birth, not in the third trimester.
explanation.pearls: Go back to the 12 week images before you quote any timing, because chorionicity cannot be assigned reliably in the third trimester and getting it wrong shifts the planned birth by a full week in either direction.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Management of monochorionic and dichorionic twin pregnancy

subtopic_detail: a low neutrophil count on clozapine in a patient whose baseline count was always at the lower limit
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar reviewing a 32 year old man of West African descent with treatment resistant schizophrenia who has been on clozapine 400 mg daily for seven months with a very good response, having failed two previous antipsychotics.

His monitoring bloods today show a neutrophil count of 1.4 x10^9/L. Looking back through the record, his neutrophil counts have run between 1.5 and 1.9 x10^9/L at every check since before clozapine was started, and a full blood count taken during an admission four years ago showed a neutrophil count of 1.6. His total white cell count has always tracked at the lower end while his lymphocytes are normal. He is afebrile, has no sore throat, mouth ulcers or other infective symptoms, and feels well.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 118/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C
data_table.Examination: No oral ulceration, no pharyngeal inflammation, no lymphadenopathy, chest clear, no focus of infection
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 1.4 x10^9/L (2.0-7.5), lymphocytes 2.1 x10^9/L (1.0-4.0), haemoglobin 148 g/L (130-180), platelets 240 x10^9/L (150-400)
data_table.Medications: Clozapine 400 mg orally daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Cease clozapine immediately and record it as a permanent contraindication for the future
options.rationale: Immediate cessation with a permanent bar is the correct response to a genuine red result, and it exists because agranulocytosis can progress rapidly to fatal sepsis. Applying it to a count that has always been at this level in this patient discards an effective treatment for treatment resistant illness on the basis of a reference range derived from a different population. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

options.text: Add lithium to raise the neutrophil count and continue the current clozapine dose
options.rationale: Lithium does raise the neutrophil count by demargination and has been used deliberately for this purpose in specialist settings. Using it to mask a count without first establishing why the count is low removes the very signal that monitoring depends on, and it is not an appropriate first response. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

options.text: Refer to haematology to confirm a constitutional low count and apply modified thresholds
options.rationale: A neutrophil count that sat at the lower limit for years before clozapine was ever started, with a normal lymphocyte count and no infections, describes a benign constitutional variant rather than drug induced marrow suppression. Haematology confirmation allows the monitoring service to register modified thresholds so that a patient who has responded to clozapine is not permanently deprived of it for a count that has never been abnormal for him. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

options.text: Halve the clozapine dose and repeat the full blood count in one week
options.rationale: Clozapine induced neutropenia is not dose related, so halving the dose does not reduce the haematological risk while it does risk losing the response that has taken seven months to achieve. Dose reduction is not part of the response to an abnormal count. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Clozapine)

options.text: Continue unchanged and repeat the count at the next scheduled monitoring interval
options.rationale: Carrying on without action ignores a result that has fallen below the threshold at which the monitoring service requires a response, and it leaves the clinician with no documented basis for the decision. Increased monitoring frequency is part of the management even when a constitutional cause is suspected. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Clozapine monitoring)

explanation.summary: Clozapine monitoring exists because of agranulocytosis, and the thresholds that trigger cessation are derived from neutrophil reference ranges based largely on European populations.
