A substantial proportion of people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry have a constitutionally lower circulating neutrophil count, caused by a normal variant affecting neutrophil margination rather than by any defect in production or in immune function. Recognising this matters because otherwise these patients are excluded from the only effective treatment for treatment resistant schizophrenia on the basis of a count that has never been abnormal for them. The evidence for the constitutional pattern here is that the low counts long predate the clozapine, that the lymphocyte count is normal, and that there is no history of recurrent infection. Haematology confirmation allows modified thresholds to be registered with the monitoring service, and monitoring continues rather than stopping.
key_points: Clozapine neutropenia thresholds derive from reference ranges based on European populations.
A constitutional low neutrophil count is common in people of African and Middle Eastern ancestry.
Counts that predate the drug, with normal lymphocytes and no infections, suggest the variant.
Haematology confirmation permits modified monitoring thresholds to be registered.
Clozapine induced neutropenia is not dose related, so dose reduction does not help.
explanation.pearls: Look for a full blood count taken years before clozapine was ever prescribed, because a neutrophil count of 1.6 in an admission four years earlier is the single piece of evidence that converts a mandatory permanent cessation into a registered modified threshold.

subtopic_detail: numb feet in a patient whose long standing medicine interferes with absorption of a vitamin
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 63 year old man with type 2 diabetes who has taken metformin 1 g twice daily for nine years. Over the past eight months he has noticed numbness and pins and needles in both feet, and more recently in his fingertips.

His most recent glycated haemoglobin was 6.8 per cent and has stayed below 7 per cent for six years. He drinks one beer on weekends and has no history of alcohol misuse. He has no back pain, no bladder symptoms and no weight loss. On examination he has reduced vibration sense to the mid shin bilaterally, absent ankle reflexes with preserved knee reflexes, and a positive Romberg test. His full blood count shows a mean cell volume of 103 fL with a normal haemoglobin, and his renal function, liver function and thyroid function are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 74/min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 15/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Reduced vibration and proprioception to mid shin, absent ankle reflexes with preserved knee reflexes, Romberg positive, no pallor, tongue normal
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 141 g/L (130-180), mean cell volume 103 fL (80-100), glycated haemoglobin 6.8 per cent, creatinine 78 micromol/L (60-110), thyroid stimulating hormone within range
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 20 mg nightly, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Arrange nerve conduction studies to characterise the distribution of the neuropathy
options.rationale: Nerve conduction studies are valuable where the pattern is atypical, asymmetrical or progressing rapidly and the diagnosis remains unclear after blood tests. They cannot identify the cause of a symmetrical sensory neuropathy, and doing them first delays a result that is available from a single tube of blood. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

options.text: Intensify glycaemic control, since neuropathy reflects inadequate long term diabetes management
options.rationale: Poor glycaemic control is the usual driver of diabetic neuropathy and improving it slows progression, which makes this a reflex answer in a diabetic patient. His control has been excellent for six years, and diabetic neuropathy does not explain a raised mean cell volume or prominent proprioceptive loss. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Diabetic neuropathy)

options.text: Measure serum vitamin B12 with folate and consider methylmalonic acid if borderline
options.rationale: Metformin reduces ileal absorption of vitamin B12 and the risk rises with dose and duration, making deficiency likely after nine years of treatment. The raised mean cell volume, the dorsal column signs with a positive Romberg test and the upper limb involvement all point away from diabetic neuropathy and toward a treatable deficiency that causes irreversible cord damage if missed. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Vitamin B12 deficiency)

options.text: Check serum protein electrophoresis and free light chains for a paraproteinaemic cause
options.rationale: A paraprotein is a recognised cause of neuropathy and belongs in the second line workup, particularly in an older patient when the common causes have been excluded. It does not account for the macrocytosis and is far less likely than the deficiency his medicine predicts. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

options.text: Request magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to exclude a compressive cause
options.rationale: Spinal imaging is indicated for asymmetrical signs, a sensory level, bladder or bowel disturbance or upper motor neurone findings, none of which he has. A symmetrical length dependent pattern with fingertip involvement does not localise to the lumbar spine. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Peripheral neuropathy)

explanation.summary: Metformin interferes with calcium dependent uptake of the vitamin B12 and intrinsic factor complex in the terminal ileum, and the resulting deficiency becomes common after several years of treatment, with risk rising with both dose and duration. Three features here argue against attributing the neuropathy to diabetes: glycaemic control has been excellent for years, the mean cell volume is raised, and the examination shows dorsal column involvement with a positive Romberg test and upper limb symptoms rather than a purely distal small fibre pattern. Deficiency is confirmed with a serum level, and methylmalonic acid or homocysteine resolve borderline results, because the serum assay is insensitive at the lower end of the range. Treatment is straightforward and neurological recovery depends heavily on how early it starts, since subacute combined degeneration of the cord becomes irreversible. Haematological abnormalities may be entirely absent even with established neurological disease.
key_points: Metformin impairs ileal absorption of vitamin B12 with risk rising over years of use.
Dorsal column signs and a positive Romberg test point away from diabetic neuropathy.
Macrocytosis may be present without anaemia, and may be absent altogether.
Methylmalonic acid or homocysteine clarify borderline serum levels.
Neurological recovery depends on early treatment before cord damage becomes fixed.
explanation.pearls: Check vitamin B12 in anyone who has taken metformin for more than four years and develops numb feet, because attributing it to diabetic neuropathy is the default that lets subacute combined degeneration progress to a deficit that replacement will never reverse.

subtopic_detail: deciding on removal versus observation for a swallowed metallic object using its position and appearance
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 3 year old girl brought in ninety minutes after her brother saw her put a coin from his money box into her mouth and swallow it. She coughed twice at the time and has been entirely well since, running around the waiting room and asking for food.

She is drooling no more than usual, is swallowing her own saliva, and has no stridor, wheeze or chest pain. Her chest and abdomen are unremarkable on examination. A single plain radiograph of the neck, chest and abdomen shows a uniform round metallic disc, about 20 mm across, lying below the left hemidiaphragm with no surrounding halo or step on either view.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 110/min, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 24/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Handling secretions normally, chest clear, abdomen soft and non tender, no subcutaneous emphysema
data_table.Investigations: Plain film shows a uniform round metallic disc 20 mm diameter in the left upper abdomen, no double ring or step off, no free gas

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange urgent endoscopic removal from the stomach within the next two hours
options.rationale: Urgent removal from the stomach is reserved for a button battery, for a sharp or elongated object, and for multiple magnets, each of which causes injury while it sits there. A single smooth coin in the stomach of a well child does none of that. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Refer for oesophagoscopy because a coin of this size lodges above the diaphragm
options.rationale: Coins of 20 mm and above do lodge more often in a small child, which is why the oesophagus must be imaged, but this one has already passed the narrow points and lies in the stomach. The site on the film, not the diameter alone, determines the risk. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Give a stimulant laxative and keep her fasted until the object has been passed
options.rationale: Laxatives do not accelerate the passage of an ingested foreign body and fasting a toddler for days is both unnecessary and unkind. Normal diet encourages normal transit. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Gastrointestinal foreign bodies)

options.text: Discharge her with advice to watch the stools and to return if pain or vomiting develops
options.rationale: A blunt object that has reached the stomach in an asymptomatic child of this size passes without intervention in the great majority of cases, so management is observation at home with clear return advice. The radiograph excludes the two appearances that would change this, a lodged oesophageal position and the double ring that identifies a battery. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

options.text: Admit for observation with repeat radiography in four hours to confirm it is moving
options.rationale: Serial films are used when an object remains in the stomach on a repeat film taken after some weeks, which is the point at which retrieval is considered. Imaging a well child again the same day exposes her to radiation without any decision depending on the result. (Source: RCH CPG: Foreign body ingestion)

explanation.summary: The two questions that decide the management of a swallowed metallic disc are where it is and what it is. An object still in the oesophagus needs removal because it causes pressure necrosis and cannot be expected to pass, whereas a blunt object that has reached the stomach passes spontaneously in almost all children. The appearance on the film distinguishes a coin from a button battery, which shows a double ring on the frontal view and a step at the edge on the lateral, and a battery in the oesophagus is a surgical emergency because it burns through the wall within hours. This child has a smooth uniform disc below the diaphragm and no symptoms, so she can go home with return advice. Repeat imaging has a role only if the object has still not passed after several weeks.
key_points: A blunt object that has reached the stomach passes spontaneously in the great majority of children.
A button battery shows a double ring on the frontal film and a step on the lateral.
A battery lodged in the oesophagus causes mucosal burns within two hours and needs immediate removal.
Sharp objects, elongated objects and multiple magnets warrant retrieval even from the stomach.
Laxatives do not speed transit and serial same day films change nothing.
explanation.pearls: Look for the double ring on the frontal film before you call anything a coin, because a 20 mm lithium battery and a coin are the same size and shade, and mistaking one for the other costs the child an oesophageal perforation within hours.

subtopic_detail: choosing between uterine sparing procedures when future pregnancy is intended
stem:
You are the registrar in the gynaecology clinic seeing a 34 year old woman with two years of increasing pelvic pressure, urinary frequency and a sensation of fullness in her lower abdomen. She and her partner intend to start trying to conceive next year.

Her periods are regular and moderately heavy but her haemoglobin is normal. She has no postcoital or intermenstrual bleeding. Examination reveals a firm irregular mass arising from the pelvis reaching to just below the umbilicus. Transvaginal and abdominal ultrasound shows a 9 cm intramural fibroid on the anterior uterine wall indenting the bladder, with a normal endometrial cavity and normal ovaries. Her cervical screening is up to date and normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Firm irregular pelvic mass palpable to just below the umbilicus, mobile, non tender, cervix normal on speculum
data_table.Investigations: Ultrasound 9 cm anterior intramural fibroid indenting the bladder, endometrial cavity normal, ovaries normal, haemoglobin 131 g/L (115-155)

lead_in: Which treatment should you recommend?

options.text: Arrange magnetic resonance imaging to exclude malignancy before any treatment is offered
options.rationale: Imaging is escalated where rapid growth after the menopause, unusual features or a suspicious ultrasound raise the possibility of a sarcoma, which is rare and cannot be excluded by imaging in any case. A typical fibroid on ultrasound in a woman of 34 does not warrant that pathway, though magnetic resonance imaging does have a role in mapping multiple fibroids before surgery. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

options.text: Insert a levonorgestrel releasing intrauterine device to control her symptoms medically
options.rationale: The device reduces menstrual blood loss effectively and is a reasonable choice where heavy bleeding is the dominant problem and the cavity is normal. It does nothing for the pressure and urinary symptoms that bulk produces, and it is contraception she does not want. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Heavy menstrual bleeding)

options.text: Refer for uterine artery embolisation as a less invasive way to shrink the fibroid
options.rationale: Embolisation is effective for bleeding and bulk symptoms and avoids surgery, which makes it attractive for women who have completed their families. It is not recommended where pregnancy is planned because of concerns about ovarian reserve, placentation and miscarriage, and because outcome data in subsequent pregnancy remain limited. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

options.text: Start a gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist for six months to shrink the fibroid
options.rationale: An agonist reduces fibroid volume and is used before surgery to correct anaemia or to make an operation more feasible, so it is an adjunct rather than a treatment. Fibroids regrow within months of stopping, and the induced hypo oestrogenic state causes bone loss and prevents conception. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

options.text: Refer for myomectomy with counselling about uterine scar risks in a future labour
options.rationale: Surgical removal of the fibroid preserves the uterus and relieves pressure symptoms caused by bulk, which is what she has, and it remains the option with the best evidence when pregnancy is intended. She needs to know that a myomectomy entering the myometrium changes the plan for a future birth and that fibroids may recur. (Source: RANZCOG: Uterine fibroids)

explanation.summary: Fibroid treatment is chosen by matching the intervention to the dominant symptom and to the woman's reproductive intentions. Bulk symptoms such as pressure, frequency and abdominal distension respond to procedures that remove or shrink the fibroid, not to medical treatments aimed at bleeding. Because she intends to conceive next year, uterine artery embolisation is avoided, since its effects on ovarian reserve and placentation and its limited pregnancy outcome data make it unsuitable when fertility matters. Myomectomy preserves the uterus and relieves bulk symptoms, at the cost of a uterine scar that influences the mode of a future birth and a recurrence rate that rises over subsequent years. A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist has a place before surgery rather than instead of it.
key_points: Match the treatment to the dominant symptom: bulk symptoms need volume reduction.
Embolisation is avoided where future pregnancy is intended.
Myomectomy preserves the uterus but creates a scar that affects future birth planning.
A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist is a preoperative adjunct, not definitive treatment.
The intrauterine device treats bleeding but not pressure symptoms.
explanation.pearls: Ask what she wants fixed and when she wants to conceive before choosing anything, because the intrauterine device and embolisation both look attractive on paper and both are the wrong answer for a woman whose complaint is pressure and whose plan is pregnancy within the year.

subtopic_detail: an analgesic bought over the counter that alters the handling of a narrow therapeutic index drug
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 46 year old woman with bipolar I disorder who has been stable on lithium carbonate 750 mg at night for six years. She has come in about low back pain after moving house and mentions that she has been taking ibuprofen 400 mg three times a day for the past ten days, bought from the supermarket.

Over the past four days she has felt nauseated, her hands have been shakier than usual, and she describes feeling unsteady on her feet. She has not vomited, has been drinking normally and has not had diarrhoea. She has had no recent dose change, no new prescribed medicines and no fevers. On examination she has a fine tremor that is coarser than her usual lithium tremor, and her gait is mildly unsteady with normal power and no focal signs.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 84/min, blood pressure 126/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Coarse bilateral hand tremor, mild gait ataxia, normal power and reflexes, no clonus, no confusion, oriented and coherent
data_table.Investigations: No bloods taken yet today
data_table.Medications: Lithium carbonate 750 mg orally at night, ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for ten days

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Switch the ibuprofen to regular celecoxib, which does not interact with lithium
options.rationale: Selective cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors act on the same renal prostaglandin pathway and raise lithium concentrations in the same way, so the substitution offers no protection. Paracetamol is the safe analgesic in this situation. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

options.text: Refer her directly to the emergency department for consideration of haemodialysis
options.rationale: Dialysis is the treatment for severe toxicity, indicated by reduced consciousness, seizures, myoclonus or renal failure, or by very high concentrations. She is alert, oriented and haemodynamically well, so the level is needed before that pathway is considered. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Lithium toxicity)

options.text: Continue both medicines and recheck the lithium level at her next routine appointment
options.rationale: Routine three monthly monitoring is appropriate for a stable patient with no new symptoms and no interacting drugs. Deferring here allows a rising concentration to continue toward the confusion, myoclonus and seizures of severe toxicity in a woman already showing neurological signs. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

options.text: Stop the ibuprofen and take an urgent lithium level with electrolytes and creatinine
options.rationale: Non steroidal anti inflammatories reduce renal prostaglandin mediated blood flow and increase proximal tubular reabsorption of lithium, raising concentrations by up to half within days, and her tremor, nausea and unsteadiness are the early features of toxicity. Removing the interacting drug and measuring the level together establish both the cause and the severity before any dose decision is made. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

options.text: Halve the lithium dose today and continue the ibuprofen until the back pain settles
options.rationale: Adjusting the lithium around an interacting drug that will be stopped in days creates a moving target and risks subtherapeutic concentrations and relapse once the anti inflammatory is finished. The interacting drug is the one to remove. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Lithium)

explanation.summary: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index and is cleared almost entirely by the kidney, so anything that reduces renal clearance raises the concentration quickly. Non steroidal anti inflammatories are the commonest culprit because patients buy them without mentioning it, and they can raise lithium concentrations by up to half within a week. The early features of toxicity are gastrointestinal upset, a coarsening of the usual fine tremor and unsteadiness, progressing to confusion, myoclonus, seizures and renal failure if unrecognised. The immediate response is to remove the interacting drug and measure the concentration alongside electrolytes and creatinine, since dehydration and renal impairment compound the effect. Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers and thiazide diuretics interact by the same renal mechanism and deserve the same caution.
key_points: Lithium is renally cleared, so anything reducing renal clearance raises the concentration.
Anti inflammatories can raise lithium concentrations by up to fifty per cent within days.
Early toxicity presents as nausea, coarse tremor and ataxia before confusion appears.
Selective cyclooxygenase 2 inhibitors interact by the same mechanism and are no safer.
Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors, receptor blockers and thiazides share the interaction.
explanation.pearls: Ask every patient on lithium what they buy at the supermarket, because ibuprofen and naproxen need no prescription, are not on the medication list you are reading, and are the commonest single cause of a lithium level that has climbed without any dose being changed.

subtopic_detail: recurrent falls where the medication list rather than a new diagnosis explains the symptom
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing an 81 year old man who has fallen four times in three months, twice in the bathroom on getting up at night and twice when standing from a chair after lunch. He has not been injured beyond bruising and has not lost consciousness.

He describes feeling lightheaded and greying out for a few seconds on standing, which resolves if he sits back down. There is no chest pain, palpitation or exertional symptom, and the episodes never happen while he is sitting or walking. He takes perindopril, amlodipine, indapamide, temazepam for sleep and oxybutynin for urinary urgency. His lying blood pressure is 142/80 mmHg falling to 108/62 mmHg after three minutes standing, with a pulse rate rising only from 68 to 74 beats per minute. His electrocardiogram shows sinus rhythm with no conduction abnormality and his neurological examination is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: Lying blood pressure 142/80 mmHg, standing blood pressure 108/62 mmHg at three minutes, pulse rate 68/min lying and 74/min standing, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal gait when observed unhurried, no cerebellar signs, proprioception intact, no cogwheel rigidity, timed up and go 14 seconds
data_table.Investigations: Electrocardiogram sinus rhythm with normal intervals, haemoglobin 137 g/L (130-180), sodium 138 mmol/L (135-145), creatinine 96 micromol/L (60-110), glucose within range
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily, amlodipine 5 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg daily, temazepam 10 mg at night, oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Arrange a 24 hour Holter monitor and an echocardiogram before changing any medicine
options.rationale: Cardiac investigation is warranted for syncope without warning, exertional symptoms, palpitations or an abnormal electrocardiogram, since arrhythmia and outflow obstruction are dangerous causes. His symptoms occur only on standing, reproduce with a documented postural drop and come with a normal trace, so the cause is already demonstrated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Syncope)

options.text: Start fludrocortisone to raise his standing blood pressure and continue the current regimen
options.rationale: Fludrocortisone has a place in orthostatic hypotension that persists after culprit drugs have been removed, usually where there is autonomic failure. Using it to counteract medicines that could simply be reduced adds supine hypertension, oedema and hypokalaemia to the problem. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.text: Request computed tomography of the brain to exclude an intracranial cause for the falls
options.rationale: Imaging is indicated after a fall with head injury on anticoagulation, with focal neurological signs or with unexplained cognitive decline. A normal neurological examination and a clear postural mechanism do not justify it, and a chronic subdural collection would not produce symptoms confined to the act of standing. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.text: Reduce his antihypertensive burden and plan a staged withdrawal of the sedative and the anticholinergic
options.rationale: A fall of 34 mmHg systolic on standing without a compensatory rise in heart rate confirms orthostatic hypotension, and three antihypertensives together with a sedative and an anticholinergic explain it entirely. Medication reduction is the intervention with the best evidence for preventing falls in this situation, and the withdrawal is staged because stopping a benzodiazepine abruptly causes its own problems. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

options.text: Refer for a falls prevention exercise programme as the single intervention needed
options.rationale: Strength and balance exercise reduces falls in older people and should form part of his plan alongside the medication review. On its own it does nothing about a blood pressure that drops 34 mmHg every time he stands up at night. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

explanation.summary: Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a fall of at least 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing, and the absence of a compensatory tachycardia here suggests the response is blunted by his medicines. Five of his drugs contribute: three lower blood pressure directly, the benzodiazepine impairs postural reflexes and increases night time falls, and the anticholinergic adds cognitive impairment and further postural drop. Medication review with staged withdrawal has the strongest evidence of any single intervention for falls of this kind, and the timing of his falls at night and after meals fits the pattern precisely. Exercise programmes, home hazard assessment and vitamin D where deficient are complementary rather than alternatives. Cardiac and neurological investigation is reserved for syncope without warning, exertional symptoms or focal signs.
key_points: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes.
An absent compensatory tachycardia suggests drugs or autonomic impairment.
Benzodiazepines and anticholinergics contribute to falls independently of blood pressure.
Medication reduction has the strongest single evidence for preventing falls of this type.
Postprandial and nocturnal timing supports a postural rather than a cardiac mechanism.
explanation.pearls: Measure lying and standing blood pressure at three minutes rather than immediately, because the drop that explains the falls frequently appears only after the first minute and a normal reading taken straight after standing sends the patient off for a Holter monitor they do not need.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Falls in older people

subtopic_detail: timing of first exposure to a high risk food in an infant whose eczema places her in the highest risk group
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 month old girl for her immunisations. Her mother mentions that she has had moderate eczema since eight weeks of age, currently controlled on a daily moisturiser and intermittent hydrocortisone 1 per cent ointment, and asks when it would be safe to give her peanut butter.

The infant has never eaten peanut or tree nuts and has never had a reaction to any food. She has had smooth cereal, pureed vegetables and yoghurt over the past three weeks without any problem. The mother has a sister with a peanut allergy and has been avoiding peanut herself while breastfeeding because she read that it would help. The infant is thriving, growth is tracking along the 50th centile, and her skin today shows mild dryness with no active flare.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Dry skin at the antecubital fossae with no excoriation or weeping, growth on the 50th centile for weight and length, no wheeze
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What advice should you give about introducing peanut?

options.text: Arrange skin prick testing to peanut and introduce it only if the result is negative
options.rationale: Testing before introduction in a child who has never reacted generates positive results that reflect sensitisation rather than clinical allergy, and acting on them delays or prevents an introduction that would have been tolerated. Testing is indicated after a reaction, not before a first exposure. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Have the mother resume eating peanut so the infant is exposed through the breastmilk
options.rationale: Maternal avoidance during breastfeeding is unnecessary and her diet can return to normal, but exposure through breastmilk is not the mechanism that induces tolerance. The infant needs to eat the food herself in a form she can manage. (Source: NHMRC: Infant Feeding Guidelines)

options.text: Defer peanut until the eczema has been clear for three months and then introduce it
options.rationale: Waiting for clear skin postpones introduction past the window in which it is protective, and moderate eczema in infancy often persists for years. Eczema raises the risk of allergy, which is a reason to introduce sooner rather than later. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Give smooth peanut paste at home in the next week and continue it regularly thereafter
options.rationale: Introducing peanut in the first year and continuing it regularly reduces the development of peanut allergy, and the benefit is greatest in infants with eczema because they carry the highest baseline risk. She has already tolerated other solids and has no history of reaction, so the introduction happens at home in the usual way with a smooth form appropriate to her age. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

options.text: Refer to an immunologist for the first dose to be given under supervised observation
options.rationale: Supervised introduction is reserved for an infant who has already reacted to that food or who has a sibling with anaphylaxis and a positive test. Routine referral for every infant with eczema would delay introduction by months and is not what the risk justifies. (Source: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention)
source_refs: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

explanation.summary: Australian guidance is that all infants should be given the common allergenic foods, including peanut and egg, in the first year of life and preferably by around six months, once solids have begun. Infants with eczema have the highest risk of food allergy and therefore stand to gain the most, so eczema is a reason to introduce earlier rather than to delay. Screening tests before a first exposure are counterproductive because sensitisation without clinical allergy is common and a positive result leads to unnecessary avoidance. Whole nuts are a choking hazard at this age, so peanut is given as a smooth paste thinned into food the infant already takes. Regular ongoing intake matters, because tolerance is maintained by continued exposure rather than by a single successful feed.
key_points: Introduce common allergenic foods in the first year, preferably around six months.
Eczema raises the risk of food allergy and argues for earlier, not later, introduction.
Screening tests before a first exposure detect sensitisation and cause unnecessary avoidance.
Whole or chopped nuts are a choking hazard until about four years of age.
Regular continued intake is needed to maintain tolerance once the food is introduced.
explanation.pearls: Tell the family to keep peanut in the diet at least twice a week after the first successful feed, because a single tolerated exposure followed by months of avoidance does not maintain tolerance and allergy can still develop.

sources.label: ASCIA: Guidelines for infant feeding and allergy prevention

subtopic_detail: the sequence of assessment after a first report of reduced movements in the third trimester
stem:
You are the midwife coordinator's registrar receiving a 26 year old woman at 32 weeks and 4 days in her first pregnancy who telephoned the assessment unit because her baby has been moving less since yesterday afternoon. She has come in immediately as advised.

She describes the movements as fewer and weaker rather than absent, and she has felt three movements in the past hour while sitting quietly. She has had no bleeding, no abdominal pain, no fluid loss and no itching. Her pregnancy has been uncomplicated, her blood pressure has been normal at every visit and her morphology scan was normal. She smokes three cigarettes a day. On abdominal palpation the uterus is soft and non tender, the presentation is cephalic, and the symphysis fundal height measures 29 cm having been 30 cm two weeks ago.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 82/min, blood pressure 114/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.7 degrees C, foetal heart rate 145/min on auscultation
data_table.Examination: Uterus soft and non tender, cephalic presentation, symphysis fundal height 29 cm at 32 weeks and 4 days, no vaginal loss on inspection
data_table.Investigations: None performed since arrival

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Give corticosteroids and admit her for continuous monitoring until the movements return
options.rationale: Corticosteroids are given when preterm birth within seven days is anticipated, which is a decision that follows the assessment rather than preceding it. Continuous monitoring at 32 weeks without an abnormal finding commits her to admission without adding information. (Source: RANZCOG: Antenatal corticosteroids)

options.text: Ask her to drink cold water, lie on her side and count movements for two hours
options.rationale: Formal movement counting protocols have not been shown to reduce stillbirth and they delay objective assessment in a woman who has already recognised a change and presented. Any manoeuvre intended to provoke movement is a substitute for the assessment rather than part of it. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.text: Arrange a biophysical profile as the single assessment and omit the cardiotocograph
options.rationale: The biophysical profile includes cardiotocography as one of its components and adds ultrasound measures of tone, movement, breathing and liquor. It takes longer to organise and does not outperform the combination of an immediate trace with a growth and Doppler assessment in this setting. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.text: Perform cardiotocography and discharge her home if the trace is normal with advice
options.rationale: A normal cardiotocograph reflects foetal wellbeing at that moment and is reassuring in the short term, which is why it is done first. It does not detect growth restriction, so discharging on the trace alone misses the pathology that reduced movements most often signal, particularly when the fundal height has fallen. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

options.text: Perform cardiotocography now and arrange a growth scan with umbilical artery Doppler
options.rationale: Reduced movements are associated with growth restriction and placental insufficiency, so assessment has two parts: immediate assessment of foetal wellbeing by cardiotocography, and assessment of growth and placental function by ultrasound. Her fundal height has fallen behind and she smokes, both of which raise the pretest probability of a small or compromised foetus, so the scan is arranged rather than considered. (Source: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

explanation.summary: Reduced foetal movement is a symptom rather than a diagnosis, and its importance lies in its association with growth restriction, placental insufficiency and subsequent stillbirth. Assessment therefore has two components that answer different questions: cardiotocography tells you how the foetus is now, and ultrasound for growth, liquor volume and umbilical artery Doppler tells you whether the placenta is failing. A normal trace is common in a foetus that is nonetheless growth restricted, so it cannot be used alone to close the episode. This woman has two additional risk factors, a fundal height that has fallen behind and ongoing smoking, which make the scan more important rather than less. Provoking movements with cold drinks or position change has no evidence base and delays assessment.
key_points: Reduced movements are associated with growth restriction and placental insufficiency.
Cardiotocography assesses current wellbeing and cannot detect growth restriction.
Ultrasound for growth, liquor and umbilical artery Doppler answers the placental question.
Symphysis fundal height falling behind or static is an indication for a growth scan.
Formal movement counting protocols have not been shown to reduce stillbirth.
explanation.pearls: Plot the fundal height against the previous measurement before deciding anything, because a static or falling height alongside reduced movements is the combination most likely to precede stillbirth and it converts a reassuring trace into an indication for a scan the same day.

sources.label: RANZCOG: Decreased fetal movements in the second half of pregnancy

subtopic_detail: separating the presence of mental illness from the capacity to refuse a specific medical treatment
stem:
You are the psychiatry registrar called to the surgical ward to see a 45 year old man with schizophrenia who is refusing an appendicectomy. The surgical team has told you he lacks capacity because of his diagnosis and has asked you to authorise the operation under mental health legislation.

He has been on paliperidone for eight years and his last relapse was six years ago. He tells you he understands he has an infected appendix, that it may burst, and that this could kill him. He says he is refusing because his brother died under a general anaesthetic three years ago and he is frightened of the anaesthetic rather than the surgery. He repeats this account consistently and can explain the trade off he is making. He has no delusions about the surgical team, no hallucinations and no thought disorder on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 98/min, blood pressure 128/80 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 38.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Right iliac fossa tenderness with guarding, mental state shows no delusions or hallucinations, speech coherent and goal directed, oriented to time place and person
data_table.Investigations: White cell count 15.2 x10^9/L (4.0-11.0), C reactive protein 88 mg/L (less than 5), computed tomography showing an inflamed appendix without perforation
data_table.Medications: Paliperidone palmitate monthly injection

lead_in: What is the most appropriate response to the surgical team?

options.text: Advise the team to proceed once he is sedated for pain, as consent will then be simpler
options.rationale: Sedating a person in order to remove their objection is a deliberate circumvention of a valid refusal and constitutes assault. Analgesia is given for pain on its own merits and never as a route around consent. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.text: Document that he retains capacity for this decision and that his refusal must be respected
options.rationale: He understands the information, retains it, weighs it against a reason that is comprehensible and communicates a consistent choice, which is all that capacity requires. A diagnosis of schizophrenia does not remove capacity, and an unwise decision made for a reason a frightened person might genuinely hold is not evidence of incapacity. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.text: Contact the guardianship board for an urgent substitute decision maker to be appointed
options.rationale: Substitute decision making is engaged when a person genuinely lacks capacity, and it is the correct pathway for non urgent treatment in that situation. Seeking it for a person who has capacity overrides a valid refusal through an administrative route and is not lawful. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

options.text: Increase his antipsychotic dose and reassess his capacity again in forty eight hours
options.rationale: Treating an illness that is currently in remission will not change a decision that is not being driven by psychotic symptoms, and forty eight hours in an inflamed appendix carries a real risk of perforation. Reassessment is appropriate when capacity fluctuates, which is not what is happening here. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Schizophrenia)

options.text: Authorise the operation under mental health legislation given the risk to his life
options.rationale: Mental health legislation authorises treatment of the mental illness itself, not unrelated surgical conditions, so it provides no lawful basis for an appendicectomy whatever the risk. Surgical treatment of a person who lacks capacity proceeds through guardianship arrangements or the emergency doctrine instead. (Source: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent)
source_refs: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

explanation.summary: Capacity is decision specific and is assessed against four elements: whether the person can understand the relevant information, retain it long enough to decide, weigh it in arriving at a choice, and communicate that choice. A psychiatric diagnosis does not by itself affect any of these, and the assessment must be made about this decision at this time rather than about the person in general. This man demonstrates all four elements and gives a reason for his refusal that is frightening but entirely rational in origin, so his refusal is valid even though the team considers it unwise. Mental health legislation cannot be used to authorise treatment of a physical condition unrelated to the mental illness. The useful clinical response is to address the specific fear, which is the anaesthetic rather than the surgery, ideally by having the anaesthetist discuss his brother's death with him directly.
key_points: Capacity requires understanding, retention, weighing and communication of a choice.
Capacity is specific to the decision and the moment, not to the person or the diagnosis.
An unwise decision is not evidence of incapacity.
Mental health legislation authorises treatment of the mental illness, not unrelated surgery.
Guardianship or the emergency doctrine applies when a person genuinely lacks capacity.
explanation.pearls: When a team says a patient lacks capacity because of a psychiatric diagnosis, ask which of the four elements is missing, because in most of these referrals the answer is none of them and the real problem is a specific fear that nobody has asked about.

sources.label: Australian Commission on Safety and Quality in Health Care: Informed consent

subtopic_detail: an evening urge to move the legs where a routine blood test changes the treatment entirely
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 55 year old woman with eighteen months of an uncomfortable crawling sensation in both legs that comes on when she sits down in the evening and is worse in bed. She has to get up and walk around, which relieves it completely until she lies down again.

She is losing about two hours of sleep most nights and is exhausted at work. The sensation is not painful and there is no burning or numbness. She has heavy periods that she has never had investigated. She takes no antihistamines, antidepressants or antiemetics. Her neurological examination is normal with intact reflexes, power and sensation, and her peripheral pulses are present. Her full blood count shows a haemoglobin of 119 g/L with a mean cell volume of 78 fL, and her ferritin is 22 micrograms/L.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Normal power, tone, reflexes and sensation in both legs, pedal pulses present, no varicosities, no calf tenderness
data_table.Investigations: Haemoglobin 119 g/L (115-155), mean cell volume 78 fL (80-100), ferritin 22 micrograms/L (30-200), transferrin saturation 14 per cent (15-45), creatinine 66 micromol/L (45-90), thyroid stimulating hormone within range
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: Start pramipexole at a low dose taken two hours before her symptoms usually begin
options.rationale: Dopamine agonists work quickly and were once first line, which is why they remain a tempting answer. Long term use causes augmentation, in which symptoms begin earlier in the day, spread to the arms and become more severe than before treatment, so they are no longer preferred and are never started before iron status is corrected. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs

options.text: Replace iron with the aim of raising the ferritin well above the lower limit of normal
options.rationale: Iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause of these symptoms because brain iron is required for dopamine synthesis, and replacement often resolves them without any specific drug. The treatment target is higher than the laboratory lower limit, around 75 micrograms per litre or more, and her heavy periods with a low mean cell volume explain the deficiency and need addressing in their own right. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

options.text: Prescribe temazepam at night to restore her sleep while the symptoms are investigated
options.rationale: Sedatives may help a patient sleep through mild symptoms and are occasionally used as an adjunct in specialist practice. They do not address the urge to move, and starting a benzodiazepine in a woman facing months of symptoms risks dependence for a condition with a treatable cause. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

options.text: Arrange overnight polysomnography to document periodic limb movements during sleep
options.rationale: The diagnosis is clinical, resting on an urge to move with an unpleasant sensation, worse at rest and in the evening and relieved by movement. A sleep study is reserved for suspected coexisting sleep apnoea or an unclear picture, and periodic limb movements are neither necessary nor sufficient for the diagnosis. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

options.text: Start gabapentin at night, titrating the dose upward according to her symptom response
options.rationale: An alpha 2 delta ligand is an appropriate pharmacological first line when symptoms persist after iron repletion, and it does not cause augmentation. Starting it now would treat the symptom while leaving the deficiency that is generating it. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Restless legs syndrome)

explanation.summary: Restless legs syndrome is diagnosed clinically from an urge to move the legs with an unpleasant sensation that is worse at rest, worse in the evening and relieved by movement. Iron status is the single most useful investigation because brain iron is a cofactor for dopamine synthesis, and deficiency is the commonest reversible cause even when the patient is not anaemic. Replacement is aimed at a ferritin well above the laboratory lower limit, commonly taken as at least 75 micrograms per litre, and often resolves symptoms without any further treatment. Where drug treatment is needed, an alpha 2 delta ligand such as gabapentin or pregabalin is preferred over a dopamine agonist, because agonists cause augmentation over time, with symptoms starting earlier in the day, spreading to the arms and becoming worse than before treatment. Contributing medicines such as antihistamines, antidepressants and dopamine blocking antiemetics are reviewed at the same time.
key_points: The diagnosis is clinical: urge to move, worse at rest and in the evening, relieved by movement.
Iron deficiency is the commonest reversible cause and occurs without anaemia.
Replacement targets a ferritin above about 75 micrograms per litre, not merely within range.
Dopamine agonists cause augmentation and are no longer first line.
Antihistamines, antidepressants and dopamine blocking antiemetics can precipitate symptoms.
explanation.pearls: A ferritin of 22 micrograms per litre is reported as only mildly low but is emphatically abnormal for this condition, where the treatment target is 75 or above, so read the number against the neurological target rather than against the laboratory range.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for restless legs

subtopic_detail: scaly scalp and flexural rash in a young infant where the absence of itch redirects the diagnosis
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 10 week old boy whose parents are distressed by thick yellowish scale that has built up over his scalp during the past month and has spread to his eyebrows and the creases of his neck. They have been told by relatives that it is eczema and that he needs a special formula.

He is exclusively breastfed, feeds well and has gained weight along the 60th centile since birth. He does not scratch, rub his head or cry when the areas are touched, and he sleeps through his night feeds. There is no family history of eczema, asthma or hay fever, and no blood or mucus in his stools. On examination the scale is greasy and adherent with mild underlying redness, there are salmon coloured patches in both axillae and the nappy flexures, and the skin elsewhere is soft with no excoriation, weeping or crusting.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Greasy adherent scale over the vertex, eyebrows and neck creases, salmon coloured patches in the axillae and nappy flexures with no satellite lesions, no excoriation, no petechiae, no hepatosplenomegaly, weight on the 60th centile
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula and stop breastfeeding for a two week trial
options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula trial belongs to suspected cow milk protein allergy, which presents with blood or mucus in the stools, vomiting, poor weight gain or an itchy eczema that fails standard treatment. Advising a thriving breastfed infant to stop breastfeeding for a rash of this appearance causes real harm for no benefit. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

options.text: Soften the scale with an emollient before washing, using a mild shampoo regularly
options.rationale: Greasy adherent scale on the scalp and face with flexural involvement in a comfortable infant who does not scratch is a self limiting condition of the first months that resolves without active treatment. Loosening the scale with an emollient such as white soft paraffin or a bath oil before gentle washing is all that is required, and the parents need to know it settles by around a year. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

options.text: Refer urgently to dermatology for skin biopsy to exclude an infiltrative condition
options.rationale: Urgent referral is warranted when a scaly scalp rash is petechial or purpuric, fails to respond to simple measures, or occurs with hepatosplenomegaly, lymphadenopathy or faltering growth, because Langerhans cell histiocytosis can present this way. A thriving infant with typical greasy scale and none of those features does not need a biopsy. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin because the thick adherent crust indicates bacterial infection
options.rationale: Bacterial infection complicating an infant rash produces honey coloured crusting, weeping, surrounding erythema and often fever, none of which is present. Greasy scale without any of those features is not an infection and antibiotics treat nothing. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

options.text: Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid to the scalp and the flexures twice daily
options.rationale: A topical corticosteroid is the treatment for atopic dermatitis, which itches intensely, spares the nappy area and appears later in infancy on the cheeks and the outer limbs. This infant does not scratch and has flexural and nappy involvement, so the diagnosis is different and a moderately potent steroid on facial and flexural skin risks atrophy. (Source: RCH CPG: Eczema)

explanation.summary: Infantile seborrhoeic dermatitis and atopic dermatitis are both common in the first year and are frequently confused, but they separate cleanly on three features. Seborrhoeic dermatitis appears in the first weeks to months, produces greasy adherent scale on the scalp, face and flexures including the nappy area, and above all does not itch, so the infant is comfortable. Atopic dermatitis appears later, itches intensely enough to disturb sleep, spares the nappy area and favours the cheeks and extensor surfaces. Getting this right matters because it determines whether the family leaves with reassurance and an emollient or with a corticosteroid, a formula change and an unnecessary interruption to breastfeeding. Referral is reserved for the infant whose scalp rash is petechial or purpuric, fails simple treatment, or comes with organomegaly or faltering growth.
key_points: Seborrhoeic dermatitis in infancy does not itch and the infant is comfortable.
It involves the nappy area and flexures, which atopic dermatitis characteristically spares.
Atopic dermatitis appears later in infancy and disturbs sleep through itch.
Treatment is emollient softening and gentle washing, and it resolves by around a year.
Petechial scale with organomegaly or faltering growth warrants urgent assessment.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the baby scratches or wakes because of the rash, because a comfortable infant with a florid scaly scalp has seborrhoeic dermatitis and needs paraffin, while an infant who rubs his face on the sheets has atopic dermatitis and needs a steroid.

sources.label: RCH Kids Health Info: Cradle cap

subtopic_detail: contraceptive choice when the reliability of an oral method is compromised by altered gut anatomy
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 31 year old woman eight weeks after a Roux en Y gastric bypass. She has lost 14 kg and wants contraception, having been told by the surgical team to avoid pregnancy for the first eighteen months while her weight is changing rapidly.

She has two children, both born vaginally, and does not want more for at least three years. Her periods are regular and not heavy. She has no history of venous thromboembolism, no migraine of any kind, and she does not smoke. Her blood pressure today is 118/74 mmHg and her current body mass index is 38. She asks whether she can simply restart the combined pill she used before the operation, since she got on well with it.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 118/74 mmHg, pulse rate 72/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 38, abdominal wounds healed, no calf tenderness or swelling, no goitre
data_table.Investigations: Pregnancy test negative, haemoglobin 124 g/L (115-155), full blood count otherwise normal
data_table.Medications: Colecalciferol, a multivitamin and oral iron as prescribed after surgery

lead_in: What contraception should you recommend?

options.text: Condoms alone, since hormonal methods are less effective at a body mass index of 38
options.rationale: Body weight does reduce the effectiveness of emergency contraception with levonorgestrel and of the contraceptive patch, so weight is a genuine consideration in method choice. Condoms have a typical use failure rate around thirteen per cent a year, which is not acceptable for a woman advised that pregnancy would be unsafe for eighteen months. (Source: RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

options.text: Restart the combined oral contraceptive pill she used successfully before the operation
options.rationale: It worked for her previously and her cardiovascular risk profile is otherwise unremarkable, which is why she is asking. The malabsorptive anatomy makes the oral route unreliable now, and the early postoperative period after a major abdominal operation is also the time of highest venous thromboembolism risk. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.text: An intrauterine device or the contraceptive implant, avoiding oral methods altogether
options.rationale: A bypass procedure shortens the absorptive surface and speeds transit, so the absorption of any oral contraceptive becomes unreliable and failure rates rise. A device or an implant bypasses the gut entirely, gives several years of cover for a woman who must avoid pregnancy for eighteen months, and does not depend on the weight loss and dietary changes still under way. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.text: The contraceptive vaginal ring, changed monthly, as an effective non oral hormonal option
options.rationale: The ring does bypass the gut and is a legitimate non oral option from an absorption point of view, so the reasoning is half right. It still delivers systemic oestrogen soon after major abdominal surgery, and it requires correct use every month rather than providing years of cover. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

options.text: A progestogen only pill taken at the same time each day with a written reminder
options.rationale: Moving from combined to progestogen only correctly removes the oestrogen and the associated thrombotic concern. It does not solve the problem, because absorption of the progestogen is affected by the same altered anatomy and this method already has the narrowest margin for a missed or delayed dose. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery

explanation.summary: Bariatric procedures divide into restrictive operations such as sleeve gastrectomy, where oral absorption is largely preserved, and malabsorptive or combined procedures such as Roux en Y gastric bypass, where the shortened absorptive surface and accelerated transit make oral medicine absorption unreliable. After a bypass, oral contraceptives of any kind are avoided and a non oral method is recommended. Long acting reversible methods suit this situation particularly well because pregnancy must be avoided through a prolonged period of rapid weight change, during which nutritional deficiencies and poor foetal growth are the concern. The early postoperative months also carry an elevated venous thromboembolism risk, which is a further reason to avoid an oestrogen containing method at this point. Women who conceive after weight loss surgery need close nutritional monitoring in pregnancy.
key_points: Malabsorptive procedures make absorption of any oral contraceptive unreliable.
Restrictive procedures such as sleeve gastrectomy largely preserve oral absorption.
Long acting reversible methods bypass the gut and cover the whole period of weight change.
The early postoperative period carries elevated venous thromboembolism risk.
Pregnancy is generally avoided for twelve to eighteen months after surgery.
explanation.pearls: Ask which operation she had before choosing a method, because a sleeve gastrectomy leaves oral contraception perfectly viable while a bypass does not, and the two are routinely described by patients in the same words as weight loss surgery.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception after bariatric surgery
RANZCOG: Management of obesity in pregnancy

subtopic_detail: choosing an antidepressant when a concurrent medicine depends on a hepatic enzyme for activation
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 52 year old woman who finished treatment for an oestrogen receptor positive breast cancer eight months ago and now takes tamoxifen 20 mg daily. She describes two months of low mood, anhedonia and poor concentration that meet criteria for a moderate depressive episode, alongside troublesome hot flushes.

She has never taken an antidepressant. She has no suicidal thoughts and no psychotic symptoms. She has no cardiac disease, her blood pressure is normal, and she takes no other medication and no herbal preparations. She has already started with a psychologist and wants medication as well because the hot flushes are waking her several times a night.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 76/min, blood pressure 124/76 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 99% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Mental state shows low mood with restricted affect, no psychomotor retardation, no psychosis, weight stable
data_table.Investigations: Full blood count, electrolytes, liver function and thyroid function all within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Tamoxifen 20 mg orally daily

lead_in: Which antidepressant is the most appropriate choice?

options.text: Fluoxetine, which is well tolerated and can be given as a single morning dose
options.rationale: Fluoxetine is a potent inhibitor of the same enzyme and carries the same concern about reduced tamoxifen activation. Its long half life also makes any later switch slower and more complicated. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Venlafaxine, which has minimal effect on the enzyme that activates her other medicine
options.rationale: Tamoxifen is a prodrug converted by cytochrome P450 2D6 to the metabolite responsible for most of its antioestrogen effect, so an antidepressant that strongly inhibits that enzyme reduces its efficacy. Venlafaxine has minimal effect on this pathway and has the additional advantage of reducing hot flushes, which is the symptom troubling her most at night. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Paroxetine, which is effective for depression and also reduces vasomotor symptoms
options.rationale: Paroxetine does reduce hot flushes and is an effective antidepressant, which is exactly why it is prescribed in this situation by mistake. It is the strongest cytochrome P450 2D6 inhibitor among the antidepressants and has been associated with increased breast cancer mortality when combined with tamoxifen. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Bupropion, which avoids sexual adverse effects and assists with fatigue and motivation
options.rationale: Bupropion has a favourable adverse effect profile in some respects but is also a strong inhibitor of the enzyme in question, so it shares the same problem. It is registered in Australia only for smoking cessation rather than for depression. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antidepressants)

options.text: Sertraline, which is first line for depression and is widely used after cancer treatment
options.rationale: Sertraline is a reasonable first line antidepressant generally and is only a moderate inhibitor of this enzyme, so it is safer than paroxetine or fluoxetine here. It still carries more interaction risk than the preferred agent and lacks the vasomotor benefit she specifically needs. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Depression)

explanation.summary: Tamoxifen is inactive as given and relies on cytochrome P450 2D6 to produce endoxifen, the metabolite that provides most of its antioestrogen activity. Antidepressants that strongly inhibit this enzyme therefore reduce the concentration of the active metabolite, and observational data have linked paroxetine in particular with increased breast cancer mortality in women taking tamoxifen. Paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion are all strong inhibitors and are avoided, while sertraline is moderate and citalopram, escitalopram and venlafaxine have minimal effect. Venlafaxine is preferred in this setting because it combines negligible interaction with useful efficacy against vasomotor symptoms, which are common on tamoxifen and are a major cause of sleep disruption. The same interaction applies to other medicines requiring this enzyme for activation, including codeine and tramadol.
key_points: Tamoxifen is a prodrug activated by cytochrome P450 2D6 to endoxifen.
Paroxetine, fluoxetine and bupropion are strong inhibitors of this enzyme and are avoided.
Venlafaxine, citalopram and escitalopram have minimal effect on the pathway.
Venlafaxine additionally reduces vasomotor symptoms.
Codeine and tramadol also require this enzyme for conversion to their active forms.
explanation.pearls: Check for tamoxifen before writing any antidepressant for a woman treated for breast cancer, because paroxetine is otherwise a sensible choice for hot flushes and it is the single worst option in this one situation.

subtopic_detail: the size of creatinine rise after starting renin angiotensin blockade that should not stop the drug
stem:
You are the general practitioner reviewing a 62 year old woman with type 2 diabetes and albuminuria who started ramipril 5 mg daily two weeks ago. She has come for the follow up blood test you arranged and feels entirely well.

Her creatinine has risen from 88 micromol/L before starting to 106 micromol/L today, and her potassium is 4.7 mmol/L. She has had no vomiting or diarrhoea, is drinking normally and has not started any anti inflammatory medicine. Her blood pressure today is 128/74 mmHg sitting, with no postural drop, and she has no oedema. Her urine albumin to creatinine ratio before starting was 42 mg/mmol. Her renal ultrasound last year showed normal sized kidneys with no obstruction and no asymmetry.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 128/74 mmHg sitting with no postural drop, pulse rate 76/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic with moist mucous membranes, no ankle oedema, no abdominal bruit, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 106 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 88, potassium 4.7 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), sodium 139 mmol/L (135-145), bicarbonate 25 mmol/L (22-32), urine albumin to creatinine ratio 42 mg/mmol
data_table.Medications: Ramipril 5 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, atorvastatin 40 mg nightly, empagliflozin 10 mg daily

lead_in: What should you do?

options.text: Halve the dose to 2.5 mg daily and recheck her renal function in four weeks
options.rationale: Dose reduction is a reasonable response when the rise approaches the threshold or when symptomatic hypotension limits treatment. Here it sacrifices part of the dose dependent reduction in albuminuria for a change that is within the expected range. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.text: Stop the empagliflozin, since it is the more likely explanation for the creatinine rise
options.rationale: Sodium glucose cotransporter 2 inhibitors do cause an initial dip in filtration rate through a similar haemodynamic mechanism, and that dip is likewise expected and reversible. Both drugs reduce kidney disease progression and neither is stopped for the anticipated early change. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Chronic kidney disease)

options.text: Arrange urgent renal artery imaging, since this degree of rise suggests arterial stenosis
options.rationale: A steep rise, often above thirty per cent and occurring within days, does raise the possibility of bilateral renal artery stenosis and warrants imaging. Her ultrasound showed symmetrical kidneys of normal size and her rise is within the expected range, so this is not indicated. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Chronic kidney disease)

options.text: Keep her on the current dose and confirm the result has plateaued on repeat testing
options.rationale: A creatinine rise of about twenty per cent reflects the expected fall in intraglomerular pressure that produces the long term kidney protection, and rises of up to thirty per cent that stabilise are acceptable and are not a reason to stop. Her potassium is within range and she is euvolaemic, so the drug continues and the result is simply confirmed as stable. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

options.text: Stop the ramipril permanently and record it as having caused acute kidney injury
options.rationale: Cessation is warranted when the rise exceeds thirty per cent, when it keeps climbing on repeat testing or when potassium rises above the acceptable range. Stopping for a stable twenty per cent rise removes the treatment that most reduces her progression to kidney failure and is the commonest error made at this point. (Source: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care)
source_refs: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

explanation.summary: Angiotensin converting enzyme inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, which lowers intraglomerular pressure and produces an immediate fall in filtration rate alongside the long term reduction in albuminuria and in progression to kidney failure. A creatinine rise of up to thirty per cent within the first two to four weeks is therefore expected and is a marker that the drug is working rather than a sign of injury. The drug is continued and the result rechecked to confirm it has stabilised. Cessation is warranted when the rise exceeds thirty per cent, continues to climb, or is accompanied by hyperkalaemia above the acceptable range, and a steep early rise raises the possibility of bilateral renal artery stenosis or volume depletion. Stopping for a stable rise within the expected range removes one of the few treatments that alters the trajectory of diabetic kidney disease.
key_points: Efferent arteriolar dilatation lowers intraglomerular pressure and raises creatinine acutely.
A stable rise up to thirty per cent is expected and the drug is continued.
Recheck renal function and potassium within two weeks to confirm stability.
A rise above thirty per cent, a continuing climb or hyperkalaemia prompt cessation.
A steep early rise suggests bilateral renal artery stenosis or volume depletion.
explanation.pearls: Calculate the percentage rise rather than reacting to the absolute number, because 88 to 106 micromol/L looks alarming on a report and is twenty per cent, which is exactly what a drug that is protecting her kidneys is supposed to do.

sources.label: KHA Kidney Disease: Chronic kidney disease management in primary care

subtopic_detail: why a scaly scalp patch with broken hairs will not respond to the treatment used for body ringworm
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 6 year old boy whose mother has been applying a topical antifungal cream to a patch on his scalp for the past four weeks with no improvement. The patch has grown and a second smaller one has appeared behind his ear.

He is otherwise well, has no fever and no pain, and attends a school where two other children have had something similar. He has no eczema and no history of hair pulling. On examination there is a 4 cm scaly patch on the vertex with hairs broken off a few millimetres above the scalp surface, a further 1 cm patch behind the right ear, and two small mobile tender nodes at the back of his neck. There is no boggy swelling and no pustulation.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Two scaly scalp patches with hairs broken close to the surface, mild occipital lymphadenopathy, no boggy mass, no pustules, no scarring, nails normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Apply a potent topical corticosteroid because the appearance suggests scalp psoriasis
options.rationale: Psoriasis produces thick silvery scale on a well demarcated plaque and characteristically spares the hair, whereas hairs broken off close to the scalp indicate the shaft itself is infected. A corticosteroid without an antifungal allows a dermatophyte to spread more widely. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Change to a stronger topical antifungal cream applied twice daily for eight weeks
options.rationale: Potency is not the problem, penetration is. No topical preparation reaches the fungal elements within the hair shaft, which is why four weeks of cream produced nothing and why another eight weeks would do the same. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Take hair and scale samples for fungal studies and begin oral griseofulvin
options.rationale: Fungal infection of the scalp sits within the hair shaft, where topical agents cannot reach, so systemic treatment for several weeks is required and topical therapy alone predictably fails. Samples are taken before treatment starts because the course runs for six to eight weeks and the species identified guides the choice and duration. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin because the tender neck nodes indicate bacterial infection
options.rationale: Reactive occipital nodes are an expected part of scalp fungal infection and do not by themselves indicate bacterial disease. A tender boggy mass with pustules would suggest the inflammatory form, which still needs an antifungal and is treated with an added corticosteroid rather than an antibiotic alone. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Dermatophyte infections)

options.text: Use an antifungal shampoo twice weekly and keep him home from school until it clears
options.rationale: Shampoo reduces surface spores and is a useful adjunct that limits spread to others, but it does not cure the infection within the shaft. Exclusion from school is not required once systemic treatment has started. (Source: RCH CPG: Skin infections)

explanation.summary: Hairs broken off a few millimetres above the scalp identify an infection inside the hair shaft rather than on the skin surface, and that anatomical fact drives the entire management. Topical antifungals cannot penetrate the shaft, so scalp disease requires an oral agent for six to eight weeks, and the four weeks of failed cream in this history is the expected outcome rather than a sign of resistance. Samples for microscopy and culture are taken before treatment because the responsible species influences the drug choice and because a long course should not rest on a clinical guess. Reactive occipital nodes are typical and do not indicate bacterial infection, while a boggy pustular mass represents the inflammatory form that additionally risks scarring alopecia. Antifungal shampoo is an adjunct that reduces transmission to household and school contacts.
key_points: Hairs broken close to the scalp indicate infection within the shaft.
Topical antifungals cannot penetrate the hair shaft and reliably fail on the scalp.
Oral treatment runs six to eight weeks and samples are taken before it starts.
Reactive occipital lymphadenopathy is expected and does not mean bacterial infection.
A boggy pustular mass is the inflammatory form and risks permanent scarring alopecia.
explanation.pearls: Any scalp scale with broken hairs and palpable occipital nodes gets an oral antifungal and a specimen, never a cream, because every week of topical treatment is a week the shaft infection keeps spreading and the culture takes up to four weeks to come back.

subtopic_detail: prepregnancy planning where the supplement dose and the medicine itself both need to change
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 26 year old woman who has been seizure free for three years on sodium valproate 800 mg twice daily for generalised epilepsy. She has stopped her contraceptive pill and says she and her husband want to start trying to conceive in the next couple of months.

She takes no other medication and has no other medical problems. She has read online that women planning pregnancy should take folic acid and has bought a supermarket multivitamin containing 500 micrograms of folic acid.
