She is otherwise well, her weight is stable with a body mass index of 24, and she has no family history of neural tube defects. She has not yet seen her neurologist about the pregnancy plan.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 24, neurological examination normal, no rash or gum hypertrophy
data_table.Investigations: None performed
data_table.Medications: Sodium valproate 800 mg twice daily, multivitamin containing folic acid 500 micrograms daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice at this visit?

options.text: Continue the current dose because three years seizure free makes a change too risky
options.rationale: Good seizure control is a genuine consideration and no change is made without a neurologist weighing it, which is why the referral is urgent rather than optional. Accepting a one in ten malformation risk without even attempting a switch is not a defensible position when effective alternatives exist. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Stop the valproate today and recheck her in four weeks to confirm she remains well
options.rationale: Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus, and an uncontrolled generalised seizure in pregnancy threatens both the woman and the foetus through hypoxia and trauma. Any change is made gradually under specialist supervision with an alternative established first. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Antiepileptics)

options.text: Advise continuing contraception and arrange urgent neurology review to change her medicine
options.rationale: Valproate carries roughly a one in ten risk of major congenital malformation and a much higher risk of impaired neurodevelopment, and both are dose related, so the priority is a planned switch to a safer agent before conception rather than after. Contraception continues during the switch because the transition takes months and an unplanned pregnancy in the interim exposes the foetus to the highest risk period. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Refer for detailed foetal morphology imaging once she conceives and change nothing now
options.rationale: Detailed imaging at 18 to 20 weeks does detect many structural malformations and will form part of her care in pregnancy. It is surveillance rather than prevention, and it cannot detect the neurodevelopmental harm that is the larger part of the risk from this drug. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

options.text: Increase her folic acid to 5 mg daily and tell her she can start trying immediately
options.rationale: The higher folate dose is correct for a woman taking an antiseizure medicine and should be started at least one month before conception. It reduces neural tube defect risk but does not protect against the other malformations or the neurodevelopmental effects of valproate, so starting it while leaving the drug unchanged addresses only part of the problem. (Source: RANZCOG: Epilepsy in pregnancy)

explanation.summary: Valproate is the antiseizure medicine with the highest teratogenic risk, causing major congenital malformation in around one in ten exposed pregnancies and impaired neurodevelopment in a substantially larger proportion, with both effects rising with dose. Because organogenesis is largely complete before many women realise they are pregnant, the change must happen before conception, which means the referral is urgent and contraception continues until an alternative is established. Women taking any antiseizure medicine also need high dose folic acid of 5 mg daily started at least a month before conception, but folate does not mitigate the non neural tube effects of valproate. Abrupt cessation is dangerous because a generalised seizure carries its own risk of foetal hypoxia and maternal injury. Detailed morphology imaging remains part of antenatal care but detects rather than prevents harm.
key_points: Valproate causes major malformation in about one in ten exposed pregnancies.
Neurodevelopmental effects are dose related and are not prevented by folate.
Women on any antiseizure medicine take folic acid 5 mg daily from before conception.
Contraception continues until an alternative medicine is established.
Abrupt withdrawal risks status epilepticus and foetal hypoxia.
explanation.pearls: Do not let the folate conversation substitute for the drug conversation: 5 mg of folic acid lowers neural tube defect risk but does nothing about the neurodevelopmental harm from valproate, which is the larger risk and the reason the neurologist needs to see her before she conceives.

subtopic_detail: aggression confined to one care task in dementia, where the trigger rather than the illness explains it
stem:
You are the general practitioner asked by a residential aged care facility to prescribe something for a 79 year old man with Alzheimer disease who has hit staff three times this month. The facility manager wants a regular antipsychotic started today.

The nursing notes show that every incident occurred during the morning shower, that all three involved the same two staff members, and that he is calm and cooperative at every other time of day including mealtimes and personal care in the evening. He has not been wandering, is sleeping through the night and has no hallucinations or persecutory beliefs described. He grimaces when his right shoulder is moved and has a documented rotator cuff problem. A urinalysis last week was negative and he is afebrile with no new medications.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 72/min, blood pressure 134/78 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Painful restricted right shoulder abduction, no delirium, attention preserved, no focal neurology, chest clear, abdomen soft
data_table.Investigations: Urinalysis negative last week, full blood count and electrolytes within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Donepezil 10 mg orally daily, paracetamol as required for pain

lead_in: What should you recommend?

options.text: Regular analgesia with a changed showering routine and review after two weeks
options.rationale: Aggression confined to one task, at one time of day, with the same staff, in a man who grimaces on shoulder movement, is a response to pain rather than a symptom requiring an antipsychotic. Regular rather than as required analgesia and a modified approach to showering address the actual trigger, and trials show scheduled analgesia reduces agitation in dementia substantially. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Prescribe as required oxazepam for staff to give before the morning shower
options.rationale: Benzodiazepines increase falls, worsen confusion and can cause paradoxical agitation in older people with dementia, and their role is confined to brief use in severe distress. Sedating a man before a painful procedure treats the staff's difficulty rather than his pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Increase the donepezil dose to address the behavioural symptoms of his dementia
options.rationale: Cholinesterase inhibitors have a modest effect on some behavioural symptoms over months and he is already at the maximum usual dose of 10 mg daily. Neither the timeframe nor the mechanism addresses aggression that occurs only during a painful task. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia

options.text: Start regular risperidone at a low dose and review the response in four weeks
options.rationale: Risperidone is the only antipsychotic registered in Australia for this indication and has a place for persistent aggression or psychosis that poses real risk after non drug measures have failed. Starting it first exposes him to an increased risk of stroke and death for a problem with an identified and treatable trigger. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia)
source_refs: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia

options.text: Send a urine sample and treat for infection while awaiting the culture result
options.rationale: New agitation in an older person does warrant a search for delirium and infection is a common cause, so the instinct is sound. His attention is preserved, the pattern is stable across weeks rather than fluctuating, he is afebrile and the urinalysis was negative, so this does not fit delirium. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Delirium)

explanation.summary: Behavioural symptoms in dementia are usually a response to something rather than a random feature of the illness, and the first step is always to look for the pattern. Aggression confined to one care task, at one time of day, with particular staff, points to that task as the trigger, and in this man the painful shoulder explains why being washed and dressed provokes him when nothing else does. Untreated pain is one of the commonest reversible causes of agitation in dementia, and scheduled analgesia reduces it substantially in randomised trials, whereas as required dosing depends on a man with dementia asking for it. Antipsychotics in this population increase the risk of stroke and death and are reserved for persistent symptoms causing real risk after non drug measures have been tried. Delirium must always be considered, but it fluctuates, impairs attention and usually has an identifiable precipitant, none of which is present here.
key_points: Behavioural symptoms are usually triggered, so identify the pattern before prescribing.
Untreated pain is among the commonest reversible causes of agitation in dementia.
Scheduled analgesia works where as required dosing fails in a person who cannot ask.
Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality risk and follow failed non drug measures.
Delirium fluctuates and impairs attention, which distinguishes it from this stable pattern.
explanation.pearls: Read the incident times and the names of the staff involved before you prescribe anything, because aggression clustered around one task at one time of day is a pain or a care approach problem, and regular paracetamol fixes more of these than any antipsychotic.

sources.label: Therapeutic Guidelines: Behavioural and psychological symptoms of dementia
Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for dementia

subtopic_detail: why a hypoglycaemic episode that has already corrected still requires admission
stem:
You are the emergency registrar seeing a 78 year old woman brought in by ambulance after her daughter found her confused and sweating at home. The paramedics recorded a blood glucose of 1.8 mmol/L and gave intravenous glucose, after which she recovered completely within minutes.

Four hours later in the department she has become drowsy again with a blood glucose of 2.4 mmol/L, which responded to a further dose of glucose. She takes gliclazide modified release 120 mg daily and metformin, and her daughter says she has been eating poorly for three days because of a sore throat. She takes no insulin. Her creatinine is 142 micromol/L, risen from a baseline of 96. She lives alone and her daughter is returning interstate tonight.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 92/min, blood pressure 124/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 18/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.9 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Drowsy but rousable during the second episode, alert between episodes, no focal neurology, mildly dry mucous membranes, chest clear
data_table.Investigations: Blood glucose 2.4 mmol/L during the second episode, creatinine 142 micromol/L (45-90) risen from 96, potassium 4.4 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), glycated haemoglobin 6.4 per cent
data_table.Medications: Gliclazide modified release 120 mg daily, metformin 1 g twice daily, perindopril 5 mg daily

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Give intramuscular glucagon and arrange review by her general practitioner tomorrow
options.rationale: Glucagon mobilises hepatic glycogen and is valuable where intravenous access is difficult, particularly in the community. Its effect is brief, glycogen stores are already depleted in someone who has been eating poorly for days, and it can provoke further insulin release in sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Sulfonylureas)

options.text: Give a carbohydrate meal and discharge her once her glucose has been stable for two hours
options.rationale: Two hours of stability is a reasonable discharge rule after hypoglycaemia caused by short acting insulin, where the effect is over and the cause is understood. It is unsafe with a long acting sulfonylurea in renal impairment, since the drug continues to stimulate insulin release long after the observation period ends. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Admit for a glucose infusion with regular monitoring and withhold the gliclazide
options.rationale: The modified release preparation acts for well over twenty four hours and her reduced renal clearance prolongs it further, so a single correction treats the reading rather than the cause and the recurrence at four hours confirms it. Admission with a glucose infusion and regular monitoring covers the many hours of continuing insulin secretion, and she cannot be observed at home with her daughter leaving tonight. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Halve the gliclazide dose and discharge her with instructions to monitor at home
options.rationale: Reducing or stopping the sulfonylurea is certainly part of the plan, and a glycated haemoglobin of 6.4 per cent indicates she is overtreated for her age in any case. Dose adjustment does nothing about the drug already circulating, which will keep causing hypoglycaemia through tonight. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

options.text: Start octreotide now as the specific antidote and observe her in the short stay unit
options.rationale: Octreotide suppresses pancreatic insulin release and is the targeted treatment for sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia, used when episodes recur despite adequate glucose. It is reserved for refractory cases rather than started at the first recurrence, and it does not remove the need for admission and monitoring. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Hypoglycaemia)

explanation.summary: Sulfonylurea induced hypoglycaemia differs from insulin induced hypoglycaemia in that the drug continues to stimulate endogenous insulin secretion for as long as it remains in the circulation, and correcting the glucose does nothing to shorten that. The modified release preparation acts for more than twenty four hours, and acute kidney injury from poor intake prolongs it further, so recurrence is the rule rather than the exception. Anyone with sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia needs admission for a glucose infusion and regular monitoring for at least twenty four hours, and longer if renal function is impaired. Octreotide suppresses insulin release and is reserved for episodes that recur despite adequate glucose replacement. A glycated haemoglobin of 6.4 per cent in a frail older woman indicates overtreatment, and relaxing the glycaemic target is part of preventing the next episode.
key_points: Sulfonylureas keep stimulating insulin release long after the glucose has been corrected.
Modified release preparations act for more than twenty four hours.
Renal impairment prolongs the effect and makes recurrence more likely.
Octreotide is reserved for hypoglycaemia recurring despite adequate glucose replacement.
A low glycated haemoglobin in a frail older person indicates overtreatment.
explanation.pearls: Never discharge a sulfonylurea hypoglycaemia from the emergency department on the strength of a normal glucose, because the drug outlasts the observation period by a day or more and the second episode typically happens overnight at home with nobody there.

subtopic_detail: treating an itchy infestation across a household where only one child has symptoms
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 2 year old girl whose parents report three weeks of an itchy rash that is much worse at night and wakes her repeatedly. Her mother has begun to notice an itch on her own wrists over the past week.

The child attends family day care. She has had no fevers and is eating and playing normally. On examination there are excoriated papules on the trunk and thin wavy tracks in the web spaces of both hands and along the inner wrists, with a few papules on the soles. Her father and her 5 year old brother have no symptoms at all. There is no weeping, crusting or surrounding cellulitis.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Linear tracks in finger web spaces and on the flexor wrists, excoriated papules on the trunk, papules on both soles, no honey coloured crusting, no fever
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat the child alone and treat other family members only if they develop an itch
options.rationale: Itch arises from a delayed hypersensitivity response that takes four to six weeks after a first infestation, so an asymptomatic contact is very often already infested. Waiting for symptoms is what produces the cycle of repeated treatment failures families describe. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

options.text: Prescribe oral ivermectin for the child as a single weight based dose
options.rationale: Oral treatment is reserved for crusted disease, for outbreaks in institutions and for people in whom topical treatment has failed or cannot be applied. It is not used as first line for ordinary infestation in a small child, where topical treatment is effective. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

options.text: Apply a moderately potent topical corticosteroid to the itchy areas for two weeks
options.rationale: A corticosteroid may be added after the infestation has been treated, because itch commonly persists for a fortnight once the mites are dead. Given alone it suppresses the inflammatory response, allows the mites to multiply and produces the widespread crusted form in a vulnerable child. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

options.text: Treat every member of the household on the same day and repeat the application in one week
options.rationale: Treating only the symptomatic child guarantees reinfestation, because contacts carry mites for weeks before itch begins, which is why the father and brother being well does not exclude them. Simultaneous treatment of the whole household with a second application a week later covers eggs that survive the first, and permethrin is applied to the whole body including the scalp and soles in a child of this age. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Scabies)

options.text: Prescribe oral cefalexin because the excoriated lesions are likely to be infected
options.rationale: Secondary bacterial infection does complicate scratched lesions and is treated when honey coloured crusting, surrounding erythema or systemic features appear. This child has excoriation without any of those signs, so antibiotics address nothing and leave the cause untreated. (Source: RCH CPG: Scabies)

explanation.summary: Night predominant itch with linear tracks in the web spaces and on the flexor wrists is the classic distribution of this infestation, and involvement of the soles is characteristic in infants and toddlers. The single most common reason treatment fails is that asymptomatic household contacts are not treated, because itch is a hypersensitivity phenomenon that takes four to six weeks to develop after a first infestation. Everyone in the household is therefore treated on the same day, whether or not they itch, and the application is repeated a week later to kill mites that hatch from eggs surviving the first treatment. In children under two the cream is applied to the scalp and face as well as the body, and to the palms and soles at every age. Bedding and clothing from the preceding days are washed hot or sealed for several days.
key_points: Itch develops four to six weeks after a first infestation, so contacts are infested before they are symptomatic.
All household members are treated on the same day regardless of symptoms.
Application is repeated after seven days to cover eggs surviving the first treatment.
In infants and toddlers the scalp, face, palms and soles are all treated.
Itch persisting up to two weeks after treatment does not indicate failure.
explanation.pearls: Warn the family before they leave that the itch will continue for up to two weeks after successful treatment, or they will return convinced it has failed and be tempted into a third and fourth application that only causes irritant dermatitis.

subtopic_detail: which investigations to order first when a couple has been trying for a year with regular cycles
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a couple who have been having regular unprotected intercourse for fourteen months without conceiving. She is 29, he is 31, and neither has children.

Her cycles are regular at 29 days with three days of moderate bleeding, no severe period pain and no pain with intercourse. She has never had pelvic inflammatory disease, abdominal surgery or an abnormal cervical screening result, and her body mass index is 23. He has no history of mumps orchitis, testicular surgery, undescended testis or chemotherapy, and he does not use anabolic steroids. Neither smokes. Her rubella serology from a previous visit shows immunity and she has been taking folic acid for three months.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 23, normal secondary sexual characteristics, no hirsutism, abdominal and pelvic examination unremarkable
data_table.Investigations: Rubella immune, cervical screening normal twelve months ago, no fertility investigations performed

lead_in: Which investigations should you arrange first?

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with dye studies to assess tubal patency and pelvic disease
options.rationale: Laparoscopy directly visualises endometriosis and adhesions and is the right investigation where there is pelvic pain, painful intercourse or a suspicious history. As a first line test in a woman with no symptoms and no risk factors it exposes her to a general anaesthetic ahead of the non invasive assessments. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

options.text: Semen analysis for him and a mid luteal progesterone for her with chlamydia testing
options.rationale: A male factor contributes in around half of couples and semen analysis is inexpensive, non invasive and abnormal often enough that it belongs in the first round for every couple. A mid luteal progesterone confirms that her regular cycles are genuinely ovulatory, and testing for chlamydia matters because previous asymptomatic infection is a common and treatable cause of tubal damage. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Sexually transmitted infections)

options.text: Advise timed intercourse with ovulation prediction kits and review again in six months
options.rationale: Advice about the fertile window is useful for couples who are mistiming intercourse, and reviewing frequency of intercourse is part of the history. Fourteen months of regular unprotected intercourse already meets the definition of infertility, so investigation is indicated now rather than after a further delay. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

options.text: Anti Mullerian hormone with a day 3 follicle stimulating hormone and oestradiol for her
options.rationale: Ovarian reserve testing predicts the response to ovarian stimulation and is therefore useful once assisted reproduction is being planned. It is a poor predictor of natural conception in a woman of 29 with regular cycles and does not explain why this couple has not conceived. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

options.text: Hysterosalpingogram now and referral to a fertility specialist for a treatment cycle
options.rationale: Tubal patency assessment is an important part of the workup and follows once ovulation and semen quality are known, since an abnormal semen analysis changes the whole pathway. Referring for treatment before any test has been done skips the step that determines which treatment is appropriate. (Source: RANZCOG: Investigation of infertility)

explanation.summary: Infertility is defined as failure to conceive after twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse, so this couple qualifies and investigation should begin rather than be deferred. The first round of tests addresses the three commonest causes in parallel: male factor, ovulatory dysfunction and tubal disease. Semen analysis is the single highest yield test because male factor contributes in about half of couples and the result changes the entire subsequent pathway. A mid luteal progesterone taken seven days before the expected period confirms ovulation even when cycles look regular, and chlamydia testing identifies a treatable and frequently asymptomatic cause of tubal damage. Ovarian reserve testing, hysterosalpingography and laparoscopy each have a place but follow this first round rather than preceding it.
key_points: Infertility is defined at twelve months of regular unprotected intercourse.
Male factor contributes in about half of couples, so semen analysis comes first.
Mid luteal progesterone is taken seven days before the expected period.
Regular cycles do not guarantee ovulation and are confirmed biochemically.
Ovarian reserve testing predicts stimulation response rather than natural conception.
explanation.pearls: Investigate both partners at the same visit rather than working through her first, because half of these couples have a male factor and a delayed semen analysis is the commonest reason a workup takes a year instead of a month.

subtopic_detail: choosing relapse prevention pharmacotherapy when the organ that clears one option is already damaged
stem:
You are the addiction medicine registrar seeing a 54 year old man on day nine of an inpatient admission who completed alcohol withdrawal management a week ago and wants medication to help him stay abstinent after discharge. He was drinking about fifteen standard drinks daily for twelve years.

He has established cirrhosis with a previous episode of ascites, and his most recent hepatic imaging showed a nodular liver with splenomegaly. He has no encephalopathy now and is fully oriented. His renal function is normal. He takes no opioids and has no chronic pain. He is motivated, has a supportive partner, has been linked with a community drug and alcohol service, and his aim is complete abstinence rather than reduced drinking.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 78/min, blood pressure 118/70 mmHg, respiratory rate 16/min, SpO2 97% on room air, temperature 36.6 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Spider naevi and palmar erythema, no ascites clinically, no asterixis, oriented with normal attention, no jaundice today
data_table.Investigations: Bilirubin 34 micromol/L (less than 20), albumin 29 g/L (35-50), international normalised ratio 1.5 (0.8-1.2), alanine aminotransferase 62 U/L (less than 40), creatinine 74 micromol/L (60-110)
data_table.Medications: Thiamine 300 mg orally daily, no other regular medicines

lead_in: Which relapse prevention medicine should you start?

options.text: Disulfiram, supervised by his partner, given his stated goal of complete abstinence
options.rationale: Disulfiram works only with supervised administration and a clear abstinence goal, both of which he has, so it is not an unreasonable thought. It is hepatotoxic in its own right and has caused fulminant hepatic failure, which makes it unsuitable in established cirrhosis. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence

options.text: No medicine, with counselling and community follow up arranged as the whole plan
options.rationale: Psychosocial treatment is the foundation of care and he is already linked with a service, so this is half of the right answer. Pharmacotherapy adds meaningful benefit on top of counselling and withholding it in a man with cirrhosis, for whom any further drinking is dangerous, is the wrong place to be conservative. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

options.text: Naltrexone, which reduces heavy drinking days and is generally better tolerated
options.rationale: Naltrexone has at least equivalent evidence in alcohol dependence and would be a reasonable first choice in a man with a healthy liver. It undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and is contraindicated in acute hepatitis and hepatic failure, and his bilirubin, albumin and clotting all indicate significant synthetic dysfunction. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

options.text: Acamprosate, with the dose set by body weight and renal function checked beforehand
options.rationale: Acamprosate is eliminated unchanged by the kidney and is not metabolised by the liver, so it is the option that remains available when hepatic function is impaired, and his creatinine is normal. Dosing is by body weight and the contraindication to watch for is severe renal impairment rather than liver disease. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

options.text: Baclofen at a low dose, titrated upward according to his response over four weeks
options.rationale: Baclofen is renally cleared and has been studied specifically in people with liver disease, which makes it a genuine second line option in this population. The evidence for it remains weaker than for the preferred agent and it carries sedation and a withdrawal syndrome of its own, so it follows rather than leads. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Alcohol use disorder)

explanation.summary: Acamprosate and naltrexone are the two first line relapse prevention medicines in alcohol dependence, and choosing between them usually comes down to organ function and the treatment goal. Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and is contraindicated in acute hepatitis and hepatic failure, while acamprosate is excreted unchanged by the kidney and is contraindicated instead in severe renal impairment. This man has cirrhosis with a raised bilirubin, low albumin and prolonged clotting, all indicating impaired synthetic function, so acamprosate is the appropriate choice and his normal creatinine confirms it is safe. Disulfiram is avoided because it is itself hepatotoxic. Concurrent opioid use is the other decisive factor, because naltrexone will precipitate withdrawal in anyone taking opioids and blocks analgesia if they are needed later.
key_points: Acamprosate is renally excreted unchanged and is not metabolised by the liver.
Naltrexone is hepatically metabolised and contraindicated in acute hepatitis or hepatic failure.
Severe renal impairment is the contraindication to acamprosate.
Disulfiram is hepatotoxic and unsuitable in established liver disease.
Naltrexone precipitates withdrawal in anyone taking opioids and blocks later analgesia.
explanation.pearls: Let the failing organ choose the drug: acamprosate for the damaged liver, naltrexone for the damaged kidney, and neither before you have asked whether the patient is taking any opioid, prescribed or otherwise.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for alcohol dependence

subtopic_detail: maintaining time critical dopaminergic dosing in a patient who cannot take anything by mouth
stem:
You are the surgical resident admitting a 72 year old man with Parkinson disease of eleven years duration who has a small bowel obstruction and is being kept nil by mouth pending theatre tomorrow. A nasogastric tube is in place on free drainage.

He takes levodopa with carbidopa at 6 am, 10 am, 2 pm, 6 pm and 10 pm, and he tells you his movement becomes very difficult within an hour of a late dose. The intern has charted his usual doses as three times daily with meals and has added metoclopramide for nausea. It is now 9 am and his 6 am dose was not given because he was in the emergency department. He is currently rigid, barely able to turn in bed and speaking softly, and he was walking independently at home yesterday.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 96/min, blood pressure 138/82 mmHg, respiratory rate 20/min, SpO2 96% on room air, temperature 37.1 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Marked rigidity with bradykinesia, soft hypophonic speech, unable to turn unaided in bed, abdomen distended with tinkling bowel sounds
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 88 micromol/L (60-110), potassium 4.1 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), abdominal computed tomography showing small bowel obstruction with a transition point
data_table.Medications: Levodopa with carbidopa five times daily, metoclopramide charted as required, nil by mouth

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate action?

options.text: Withhold all his medicines until after theatre and restart them when he is eating again
options.rationale: Withholding oral medicines is standard for most drugs before an operation and is what the nil by mouth order is usually taken to mean. Levodopa is a specific exception because interruption for even a day risks an akinetic crisis, aspiration and a syndrome resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Convert him to a rotigotine patch at an equivalent dose and leave the metoclopramide charted
options.rationale: A transdermal dopamine agonist is the accepted alternative when no enteral route is available at all, and calculating the equivalent dose requires specialist input. He has a working nasogastric tube, and leaving a centrally acting dopamine antagonist charted undermines whatever dopaminergic treatment is given. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Accept the three times daily charting as close enough and give the doses with the drug round
options.rationale: Standard ward drug rounds are convenient and adequate for most medicines, which is exactly how this error is made. In advanced disease the interval between doses determines whether the patient can move at all, and shifting a five times daily schedule onto the ward round produces hours of immobility each day. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

options.text: Give intravenous apomorphine as a bolus now and reassess his rigidity in thirty minutes
options.rationale: Apomorphine is a potent dopamine agonist given subcutaneously rather than intravenously, and it is used for sudden off periods under specialist supervision with premedication against severe vomiting. It is not a ward level substitute for restoring the regular schedule. (Source: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease)
source_refs: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease

options.text: Give the levodopa through the nasogastric tube at his exact home times and cease the metoclopramide
options.rationale: Missed or delayed doses in advanced Parkinson disease cause rapid deterioration and can precipitate an akinetic crisis with rigidity, swallowing failure and aspiration, so the home schedule is maintained through the tube with the tube clamped briefly after each dose. Metoclopramide is a dopamine antagonist that crosses into the brain and will worsen his rigidity, so it is replaced with an antiemetic that does not. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Parkinson disease)

explanation.summary: Levodopa has a short plasma half life and in advanced Parkinson disease the response follows the dosing schedule closely, so delays of even an hour produce disabling off periods. Interrupting treatment altogether can precipitate an akinetic crisis, with severe rigidity, inability to swallow, hyperthermia and a picture resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, which carries a real mortality. A nil by mouth order therefore does not extend to levodopa, which is given through a nasogastric tube at the patient's own times, or delivered by a rotigotine patch when no enteral route exists. Dopamine antagonists must be avoided, so metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol are replaced by ondansetron or domperidone for nausea and by quetiapine if an antipsychotic is unavoidable. Charting the home regimen exactly, rather than mapping it onto standard ward drug rounds, is the single most important prescribing decision at admission.
key_points: Levodopa has a short half life and the dosing schedule determines mobility.
Interruption can precipitate an akinetic crisis resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome.
Nil by mouth does not include levodopa, which is given by nasogastric tube.
A rotigotine patch is the alternative when no enteral route is available.
Metoclopramide, prochlorperazine and haloperidol are avoided as central dopamine antagonists.
explanation.pearls: Chart the patient's own times rather than three times daily on admission, and cross off any metoclopramide, because those two entries on the drug chart cause more avoidable deterioration in Parkinson disease than anything that happens in theatre.

sources.label: Australian Medicines Handbook: Drugs for Parkinson disease

subtopic_detail: bone deformity in a toddler where the dietary and sun exposure history points away from a physiological cause
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 20 month old boy whose mother is worried that his legs have become more bowed rather than less over the past six months, and that he is slow to walk any distance.

He was born at term and is still breastfed four times a day with small amounts of family food. The family covers up outdoors for cultural reasons and rarely spends time in direct sunlight. He has had no fractures and no bone pain that the family has noticed, and his bowels are regular with no diarrhoea or greasy stools. On examination he has symmetrical bowing of both tibiae, palpable widening at both wrists, and a row of small bony prominences along the costochondral junctions. His height has fallen from the 50th to the 10th centile over the past year while his weight has stayed on the 25th.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical tibial bowing, widened wrists, costochondral prominences, delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, waddling gait, height dropping across centiles
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial investigation?

options.text: Measure calcium, phosphate, alkaline phosphatase, vitamin D and parathyroid hormone
options.rationale: Wrist widening and costochondral prominences are the signs of unmineralised growth plate rather than of physiological bowing, and this biochemical panel confirms the metabolic pattern and shows how far it has progressed. A raised alkaline phosphatase with a low phosphate and a raised parathyroid hormone identifies the deficiency state and distinguishes it from the inherited phosphate wasting forms. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Send coeliac serology with total immunoglobulin A as the first line test
options.rationale: Malabsorption is a genuine cause of this bone disease and coeliac serology belongs in the workup if the first line biochemistry is abnormal and the dietary history does not explain it. Here the combination of prolonged breastfeeding with minimal solids and near complete sun avoidance explains the deficiency directly, and his stools are normal. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Arrange a bone density scan to quantify the degree of bone loss
options.rationale: Densitometry in a toddler is difficult to interpret because results must be corrected for bone size and skeletal maturity, and it does not distinguish the cause. The diagnosis here is biochemical and radiographic, not densitometric. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Start high dose oral vitamin D now and reassess the legs in three months
options.rationale: Treatment is indeed high dose vitamin D with adequate calcium intake, but starting before baseline biochemistry removes the ability to confirm the diagnosis and to detect the inherited phosphate wasting forms that will not respond. Baseline results also allow the response to be measured. (Source: RCH CPG: Vitamin D deficiency)

options.text: Request standing long leg radiographs to measure the tibiofemoral angle
options.rationale: Alignment films are used when bowing is the only abnormality and the question is physiological bowing against a growth plate disorder of one side. Wrist widening, rib changes and height crossing centiles have already moved this beyond an alignment problem. (Source: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

explanation.summary: Physiological bowing is symmetrical, painless and improves after the second birthday, and it is not accompanied by changes elsewhere in the skeleton. Widening at the wrists, prominences along the costochondral junctions, a delayed fontanelle and height crossing centiles all point instead to failure of mineralisation at the growth plate. The risk factors here are prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation beyond six months, minimal dietary intake and almost no ultraviolet exposure, which together deplete vitamin D stores. Baseline biochemistry confirms the metabolic picture and separates nutritional deficiency, in which parathyroid hormone rises and phosphate falls, from the inherited phosphate wasting disorders that require a different treatment. Treatment follows the results and is high dose vitamin D with adequate calcium, since replacing vitamin D alone in a child with poor calcium intake gives an incomplete response.
key_points: Wrist widening and costochondral prominences distinguish metabolic bone disease from physiological bowing.
Physiological bowing is symmetrical and improves after about two years of age.
Prolonged breastfeeding without supplementation plus minimal sun exposure depletes vitamin D stores.
A raised alkaline phosphatase with low phosphate and raised parathyroid hormone indicates the deficiency state.
Calcium intake must be adequate or vitamin D replacement alone gives an incomplete response.
explanation.pearls: Run your thumb along the costochondral junctions of any toddler with bowed legs, because a palpable row of beads turns an orthopaedic referral into a blood test and a treatable deficiency that also affects the mother and the next baby.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Bow legs and knock knees

subtopic_detail: the headache feature that makes combined hormonal contraception unacceptable rather than merely cautious
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman who wants to start the combined oral contraceptive pill because her friend found it helped her skin. She has no children and does not want to conceive for several years.

She describes headaches about once a month, each preceded for twenty minutes by a shimmering zigzag in her right visual field, followed by a throbbing left sided headache with nausea and light sensitivity lasting most of a day. The visual disturbance resolves completely before the headache begins. She does not smoke, her blood pressure today is 112/70 mmHg, and her body mass index is 22. She has no personal or family history of venous thromboembolism or stroke, and she takes no regular medication.

data_table.Vital signs: Blood pressure 112/70 mmHg, pulse rate 68/min, other observations within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Body mass index 22, neurological examination normal between episodes, visual fields full to confrontation, fundoscopy normal
data_table.Investigations: None performed
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What contraception should you recommend?

options.text: A progestogen only method such as the implant, the intrauterine device or the pill
options.rationale: Focal neurological symptoms preceding a headache and resolving before it starts identify migraine with aura, which raises ischaemic stroke risk, and combined hormonal contraception multiplies that risk further, so it is unacceptable regardless of age or other risk factors. Progestogen only methods carry no such stroke association and are unrestricted in these women, which leaves her the full range of long acting and oral options. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.text: A low dose combined pill containing 20 micrograms of ethinyloestradiol with monitoring
options.rationale: Lowering the oestrogen dose reduces venous thromboembolism risk but does not remove the arterial risk that matters here, and no dose of oestrogen is considered acceptable alongside aura. Monitoring cannot detect an impending stroke. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.text: A combined pill taken continuously, since her headaches occur in the hormone free week
options.rationale: Continuous regimens genuinely reduce the oestrogen withdrawal headaches that occur in the hormone free interval, which is useful for migraine without aura. That strategy does not apply to a woman who should not be taking oestrogen at all, and her headaches currently occur without any hormonal cycling. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Migraine)

options.text: Copper intrauterine device only, because hormonal contraception is unsafe in migraine
options.rationale: The copper device is a perfectly reasonable option for her and carries no hormonal risk at all. Restricting her to it alone misstates the evidence, because it is oestrogen rather than hormonal contraception in general that is contraindicated, and it may worsen the heavy bleeding some women experience. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

options.text: A combined vaginal ring, since non oral delivery avoids the first pass hepatic effect
options.rationale: Route of administration changes hepatic exposure and some metabolic effects, but the systemic oestrogen and the arterial risk remain, so the ring and the patch are restricted in exactly the same way as the pill. The contraindication follows the hormone rather than the delivery method. (Source: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine)
source_refs: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

explanation.summary: Aura is defined by fully reversible focal neurological symptoms that develop over several minutes and precede or accompany the headache, most often visual and most often described as zigzag lines or a shimmering scotoma. Its importance in contraceptive prescribing is that migraine with aura roughly doubles ischaemic stroke risk, and combined hormonal contraception multiplies that risk further, so oestrogen containing methods are unacceptable at any age and any dose. The restriction applies to the pill, the patch and the ring equally, because it follows the systemic oestrogen rather than the route. Progestogen only methods and the copper intrauterine device carry no such association and are all available to her. Migraine without aura is treated differently and combined contraception can usually be used with review.
key_points: Aura consists of fully reversible focal symptoms developing over minutes before the headache.
Migraine with aura roughly doubles ischaemic stroke risk.
Combined hormonal contraception is unacceptable with aura at any oestrogen dose.
The restriction applies equally to the pill, the patch and the ring.
Progestogen only methods and the copper device carry no arterial risk restriction.
explanation.pearls: Ask whether the visual symptom comes before the headache and goes away completely, because photophobia and blurred vision during a migraine are not aura, while twenty minutes of zigzag lines beforehand rules out every oestrogen containing method she might ask for.

sources.label: Family Planning Alliance Australia: Contraception and migraine

subtopic_detail: the timing that determines whether the first dose relieves withdrawal or precipitates it
stem:
You are the registrar at a community drug and alcohol service starting a 29 year old man on buprenorphine with naloxone for heroin dependence. He has been injecting about half a gram daily for four years and has agreed to opioid treatment after a friend died of an overdose.

He arrives at 9 am having used heroin at 7 am this morning, saying he wanted to be comfortable for the appointment. He denies methadone or other long acting opioid use. He is not sweating, his pupils are small, he has no yawning, gooseflesh, abdominal cramps, rhinorrhoea or muscle aches, and he is comfortable sitting in the chair. His urine drug screen is positive for opioids only, and his hepatitis and human immunodeficiency virus screening is pending.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 68/min, blood pressure 118/72 mmHg, respiratory rate 14/min, SpO2 98% on room air, temperature 36.5 degrees C
data_table.Examination: Pupils 2 mm and reactive, skin dry and warm, no piloerection, no rhinorrhoea, no tremor, alert and comfortable
data_table.Investigations: Urine drug screen positive for opioids only, liver function tests within normal limits
data_table.Medications: Nil prescribed

lead_in: What should you do now?

options.text: Delay the first dose until objective withdrawal features are present, reviewing him later today
options.rationale: Buprenorphine is a partial agonist with very high receptor affinity, so giving it while receptors are still occupied by a full agonist displaces that agonist and causes an abrupt and severe precipitated withdrawal. Waiting until objective signs such as dilated pupils, gooseflesh, sweating and rhinorrhoea are present confirms the receptors are free enough for the first dose to relieve symptoms rather than provoke them. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.text: Start methadone today instead, since the recent heroin use makes it the safer option
options.rationale: Methadone is a full agonist and does not precipitate withdrawal, so it can be started without waiting, which makes it a legitimate alternative for someone who cannot tolerate the wait. It carries a substantially higher overdose risk during induction because of accumulation over the first days, so it is a considered choice rather than the default when timing is the only obstacle. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.text: Admit him for a naltrexone implant instead, given his high risk of fatal overdose
options.rationale: Naltrexone is an antagonist used after complete detoxification and requires a full opioid free interval beforehand, so it cannot be started today either. Relapse after antagonist treatment also carries a high mortality because tolerance has been lost. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Opioid dependence)

options.text: Give the first dose now with an antiemetic and clonidine to cover any reaction
options.rationale: Symptomatic medicines take the edge off ordinary withdrawal and have a role alongside induction. They do not prevent or adequately treat precipitated withdrawal, which is far more severe than spontaneous withdrawal and frequently ends a person's engagement with treatment altogether. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

options.text: Give a reduced first dose now and repeat it in four hours if he tolerates it
options.rationale: Dose reduction is used to make an induction gentler once the timing is right and withdrawal has begun. It does not prevent precipitated withdrawal, because the reaction is driven by displacement of the full agonist rather than by the size of the dose. (Source: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence)
source_refs: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

explanation.summary: Buprenorphine binds opioid receptors with higher affinity than heroin or morphine but activates them only partially, so administering it while a full agonist is still bound displaces that agonist and drops receptor activation sharply. The result is precipitated withdrawal, which comes on within an hour, is more severe than spontaneous withdrawal and often destroys a person's willingness to try treatment again. The safeguard is timing rather than dose: the first dose is given only once objective withdrawal signs are present, typically six to twelve hours after short acting opioids and considerably longer after methadone. Objective signs such as dilated pupils, piloerection, sweating and rhinorrhoea are what count, since subjective craving and anxiety appear far earlier. This man used two hours ago, has pinpoint pupils and no objective signs, so dosing now would reliably produce the reaction.
key_points: Buprenorphine has higher receptor affinity than full agonists but only partial activity.
Dosing while a full agonist is bound displaces it and precipitates withdrawal.
Wait for objective signs, typically six to twelve hours after short acting opioids.
Longer intervals are needed after methadone or other long acting opioids.
Reducing the dose does not prevent the reaction, since displacement drives it.
explanation.pearls: Look at the pupils before the first dose, because a patient reporting that he feels terrible with 2 mm pupils and dry skin is anxious rather than in withdrawal, and dosing him then produces the one experience most likely to stop him ever coming back.

sources.label: Australian national guidelines for medication assisted treatment of opioid dependence

subtopic_detail: resisting acid suppression in a thriving infant whose vomiting distresses the parents more than the child
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 3 month old boy whose parents describe vomiting after almost every feed since about three weeks of age. They have been given a proton pump inhibitor prescription by an after hours service and want your view before starting it.

The vomiting is effortless, happens within twenty minutes of a feed, and is milk that looks unchanged. He does not arch, scream or refuse feeds, and he settles quickly afterwards. There is no blood or green colour in the vomit, no constipation and no fevers. He is formula fed, taking 180 mL every three hours, which the parents have been increasing because they assume he is bringing most of it back up. His weight has tracked steadily along the 75th centile since birth, and examination including the abdomen is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse rate 132/min, respiratory rate 40/min, SpO2 99% in air, temperature 36.8 degrees C, blood pressure not indicated
data_table.Examination: Alert and settled, abdomen soft with no mass, anterior fontanelle normal, weight on the 75th centile tracking since birth, no dehydration
data_table.Investigations: None performed
data_table.Medications: Nil regular

lead_in: What is the most appropriate advice?

options.text: Change to an extensively hydrolysed formula for a two week trial of dairy exclusion
options.rationale: A hydrolysed formula trial is reasonable where vomiting occurs with blood or mucus in the stools, eczema, faltering growth or marked feed refusal, since cow milk protein allergy can mimic reflux. None of those features is present and a formula change adds cost and complexity without a target. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

options.text: Explain the natural history, reduce the feed volume per feed and do not start the medicine
options.rationale: Effortless vomiting of unchanged milk in a thriving infant who feeds happily is a normal developmental phenomenon that resolves as the infant spends more time upright and takes solids. He is being offered around 200 mL per kilogram per day, well above requirement, and overfeeding is the reversible driver here, so reducing the volume per feed while keeping the frequency is the intervention that works. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

options.text: Advise raising the head of the cot and putting him down to sleep on his left side
options.rationale: Positional measures reduce measured reflux episodes but any sleep position other than supine increases the risk of sudden unexpected death in infancy, so the trade is not acceptable. Cot elevation has not been shown to reduce symptoms and can cause the infant to slide into an unsafe position. (Source: Red Nose Australia: Safe sleeping)

options.text: Request an abdominal ultrasound to assess the pylorus before changing anything
options.rationale: Pyloric stenosis presents with forceful vomiting during or straight after a feed in a hungry infant who loses weight, and it declares itself between two and eight weeks. Effortless vomiting with steady growth at three months does not fit that pattern. (Source: RCH CPG: Vomiting in infants)

options.text: Start the proton pump inhibitor for a four week trial and review the response
options.rationale: Trials in infants show acid suppression does not reduce crying or vomiting more than placebo, and it is associated with increased gastrointestinal and respiratory infection. Its place is in proven oesophagitis or in reflux with faltering growth, neither of which describes a settled infant on the 75th centile. (Source: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants)
source_refs: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

explanation.summary: Effortless posseting of unchanged milk in an infant who feeds willingly, settles afterwards and grows along a centile is physiological and needs explanation rather than treatment. The feed volume matters: 180 mL every three hours in a baby of this age is well above the usual requirement of about 150 mL per kilogram per day, and overfeeding is one of the few reversible contributors. Acid suppression has repeatedly failed to outperform placebo for crying and vomiting in infants and carries a real infection risk, so it is reserved for proven oesophagitis or for reflux with faltering growth. Features that should redirect the assessment include bile or blood in the vomit, faltering growth, feed refusal, blood in the stools and fever. Side or prone sleeping is never recommended because the risk of sudden unexpected death outweighs any reduction in reflux.
key_points: Effortless vomiting with normal growth and settled behaviour needs explanation, not treatment.
Requirement is about 150 mL per kilogram per day and exceeding it worsens posseting.
Acid suppression does not outperform placebo for infant crying or vomiting.
Bile, blood, faltering growth, fever or feed refusal each redirect the assessment.
Supine sleeping is maintained regardless of reflux because of sudden death risk.
explanation.pearls: Work out the millilitres per kilogram per day before you write anything, because a baby taking over 200 mL per kilogram daily will keep vomiting on any dose of any acid suppressant, and reducing the volume per feed usually settles it within a week.

sources.label: RCH CPG: Gastro oesophageal reflux in infants

subtopic_detail: whether laparoscopy is needed before treating cyclical pelvic pain with a typical history
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing a 24 year old woman with four years of pelvic pain that begins two days before each period, continues through the heaviest days, and has recently started to occur with deep penetration during intercourse. She misses one or two days of work most months.

Ibuprofen taken when the pain is already severe helps a little. She has never been pregnant, does not want to conceive for at least four years and currently uses condoms. There is no bleeding between periods, no bowel or bladder symptoms, and no fevers or weight loss. Her mother had a hysterectomy in her thirties for pelvic pain. Examination shows a mobile anteverted uterus with mild tenderness in the posterior fornix and no palpable mass or nodularity. Pelvic ultrasound reports normal ovaries with no endometrioma.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Anteverted mobile uterus, mild posterior fornix tenderness, no adnexal mass, no palpable nodularity, speculum examination normal
data_table.Investigations: Transvaginal ultrasound normal ovaries with no endometrioma, chlamydia nucleic acid test negative, full blood count normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first treatment?

options.text: A gonadotropin releasing hormone agonist with add back hormone therapy for six months
options.rationale: Agonist treatment is effective and is used when first line hormonal treatment has failed or is not tolerated, with add back therapy to limit bone loss and vasomotor symptoms. Starting with it in a woman who has not yet tried simpler options exposes her to those adverse effects unnecessarily. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Refer to a pelvic pain physiotherapist and a psychologist as the initial management plan
options.rationale: Pelvic floor physiotherapy and pain psychology are genuinely valuable in persistent pelvic pain and belong in the longer term plan, particularly where central sensitisation has developed. Offering them instead of hormonal suppression at the first visit withholds the treatment that addresses the cyclical mechanism driving her pain. (Source: Therapeutic Guidelines: Endometriosis)

options.text: Diagnostic laparoscopy with excision of any lesions before starting medical treatment
options.rationale: Laparoscopy establishes the diagnosis histologically and treats lesions at the same time, and it is appropriate where medical treatment has failed, where fertility is an immediate concern or where deep disease is suspected. Requiring it before any treatment delays relief by months and exposes a young woman to surgery she may never need. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging of the pelvis to stage the disease before choosing treatment
options.rationale: Imaging is valuable for mapping deep infiltrating disease and endometrioma before surgery, and transvaginal ultrasound by an experienced operator detects much of this. Superficial peritoneal disease is invisible on all imaging, so a normal scan neither excludes the condition nor changes the first line medical plan. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

options.text: Continuous combined hormonal contraception with a regular anti inflammatory before pain starts
options.rationale: Suppressing ovulation and menstruation treats the cyclical pain of this condition and is offered on the clinical picture without waiting for surgical confirmation, since laparoscopy is no longer required to begin treatment. Taking the anti inflammatory regularly from before the pain begins works far better than taking it once the pain is established, and she also gains the contraception she currently lacks. (Source: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis)
source_refs: RANZCOG: Australian clinical practice guideline for the diagnosis and management of endometriosis

explanation.summary: Cyclical pelvic pain beginning before the period, continuing through it and accompanied by deep pain during intercourse is a typical history for endometriosis, and a normal ultrasound does not argue against it because superficial peritoneal disease cannot be seen on any imaging. Australian guidance has moved away from requiring laparoscopic confirmation before treatment, so medical management is started on the clinical picture and the diagnosis is supported by the response. Continuous combined hormonal contraception suppresses ovulation and menstruation and addresses the cyclical mechanism, and it suits a woman who also needs contraception. Anti inflammatories work best taken regularly from before the pain begins rather than as rescue once it is established. Surgery, agonist therapy and multidisciplinary pain management all remain available if this approach fails or if fertility becomes the presenting issue.
key_points: A normal pelvic ultrasound does not exclude superficial peritoneal disease.
Treatment is started on the clinical picture without requiring laparoscopic confirmation.
Continuous hormonal suppression targets the cyclical mechanism of the pain.
Anti inflammatories are most effective taken regularly from before the pain starts.
Agonist therapy with add back is reserved for failure of first line hormonal treatment.
explanation.pearls: Tell her to start the anti inflammatory the day before her period is due rather than when the pain arrives, because prostaglandin release has already happened by the time she reaches for the tablet and that single change in timing often doubles the benefit she gets from it.

subtopic_detail: night waking maintained by the conditions under which a toddler falls asleep
stem:
You are the general practitioner seeing the exhausted mother of a 2 year old girl who wakes three or four times every night and will not resettle unless a parent lies on the floor beside her cot until she is asleep again. This has been the pattern for eight months and the mother is now falling asleep at work.

The child falls asleep at bedtime only with a parent lying next to her. She snores only with colds, has never been seen to stop breathing, and has no mouth breathing or daytime sleepiness. She naps once for an hour in the early afternoon, is dry overnight, has no pain, and her tonsils are not enlarged. Growth and development are normal and her behaviour during the day is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: Vital signs within normal limits
data_table.Examination: Tonsils small, no adenoidal facies, nasal airway clear, ears normal, growth and development appropriate for age
data_table.Investigations: None performed

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure the mother that this resolves with age and review again in six months
options.rationale: Learned sleep associations of this kind persist for years without intervention rather than resolving on their own, and the maternal sleep deprivation described is itself a safety issue at work and on the road. Reassurance without a plan leaves a treatable problem in place. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Teach a graduated settling approach so she learns to fall asleep without a parent present
options.rationale: She wakes normally between sleep cycles as every toddler does, but she can only return to sleep by recreating the conditions present when she first fell asleep, which is a parent lying beside her. Changing what happens at bedtime is therefore the intervention that changes the night waking, and graduated settling with progressively delayed responses has the strongest evidence in this age group. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Prescribe melatonin at bedtime for four weeks to consolidate the overnight sleep
options.rationale: Melatonin shortens the time taken to fall asleep and has a place in neurodevelopmental conditions where the sleep phase is genuinely delayed. It does not address a learned sleep association and does not reduce night waking of this type, and it is not first line in an otherwise well toddler. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

options.text: Refer for overnight sleep study to assess for obstructive sleep apnoea
options.rationale: A sleep study is directed at habitual snoring, witnessed pauses, mouth breathing, restless sleep with sweating or daytime behavioural change. Snoring only with intercurrent colds and a clear airway on examination does not meet that threshold. (Source: RCH CPG: Obstructive sleep apnoea)

options.text: Advise dropping the daytime nap so that she builds more sleep pressure by bedtime
options.rationale: One early afternoon nap is developmentally appropriate at two years and removing it usually produces an overtired child who settles worse. Nap timing matters if the nap runs late into the afternoon, which is not the case here. (Source: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children)
source_refs: RCH Kids Health Info: Sleep problems in children

explanation.summary: Brief arousals between sleep cycles happen in every young child several times a night, and whether they become a presenting problem depends on what the child needs in order to fall back asleep. A child who falls asleep at bedtime with a parent beside her requires that same parent at each arousal, which converts normal physiology into repeated calls for help. The effective intervention therefore targets bedtime rather than the night waking itself, teaching the child to fall asleep independently through graduated settling with progressively longer intervals before responding. Snoring only during colds, a clear nasal airway and small tonsils argue against obstructive sleep apnoea, which is the differential that would require a very different pathway. Parental exhaustion of this degree deserves acknowledgement in its own right and makes deferral an unsatisfactory answer.
key_points: Night waking becomes a problem when the child cannot return to sleep unaided.
The conditions present at sleep onset must be recreated at each normal arousal.
Graduated settling targets bedtime and has the strongest evidence at this age.
Habitual snoring, witnessed pauses or mouth breathing indicate assessment for obstructive sleep apnoea.
A single early afternoon nap remains developmentally appropriate at two years.
explanation.pearls: Ask exactly what is happening in the room at the moment the child first falls asleep, because that detail predicts what she will demand at two in the morning better than anything else in the history, and changing it is what fixes the nights.
